pipelines.source: Eric Tech, Claude Code: The Complete AI-Native SDLC Guide (YouTube walkthrough of Anthropic's 14-lesson Claude Academy course The AI-native SDLC playbook)

stages.name: Plan
stages.what_happens: The agent interviews the idea owner with a grilling skill, going down the decision tree branch by branch until both share the same understanding. It then writes intent.md from a template: title, problem, proposed outcome, affected users, constraints, open questions. You can trigger it as a command or skill at the end of the grilling session.
stages.who: mix: human answers, agent interviews and writes
inputs: ticket or production alert when the loop restarts
outputs: intent.md (one per change, in an intent/ folder or in the ticket system such as Jira, GitHub Projects or Linear via MCP)
stages.human_gate: Human answers and corrects the intent. Anthropic's course adds a product owner who approves intent.md or closes it; the video leaves this implicit.

stages.name: Design
stages.what_happens: The agent turns intent.md into spec.md. intent.md holds the why; spec.md holds the what: technical requirements and expected behaviour. Anthropic provides a prompt for this; Matt Pocock or Superpowers spec skills work too. Per the Anthropic source, team rules (brand, security, compliance, UX) are written as skills, and the agent flags rules that conflict.
stages.human_gate: Spec approval. The course names the product owner; that approval starts the build.

stages.name: Build: plan
stages.what_happens: The agent turns intent plus spec into plan.md: title, which files change and where, order of work, risks, and how completion is proven (tests). Tasks can run in parallel or in sequence. Alternatives: Matt Pocock's to-tickets skill, Superpowers writing-plans (goal, architecture, tech stack, global constraints, tasks with files, interfaces and checkboxes). Per Anthropic, Claude writes it in read-only plan mode.
stages.human_gate: Plan approval before any code (explicit in the Anthropic source: nothing is built until someone approves the plan).

stages.name: Build and Test (TDD self-check loop)
stages.what_happens: Tests are written before the code. The agent then iterates until three checks are green: tests, lint and build (build means it compiles and runs, not coding). Instruction: do not report done until all three are green. Feedback can also be a screenshot. Test layers: unit tests (Jest, Vitest), then component tests (React Testing Library), then end-to-end tests (Cypress, Playwright).
stages.who: agent, with deterministic tools (test runner, linter, compiler)
outputs: passing test, lint and build output as proof
stages.human_gate: none until the checks are green; the human steps in afterwards

stages.name: Continuous evals in CI
stages.what_happens: Turn 20 to 50 real tasks the agent already completed (past PRs or issues) into evals: a prompt plus the expected output, built with a skill such as skill-creator. A GitHub workflow (agent-eval) runs Claude headless with an allowed tool list and reruns the evals whenever the model, a skill or a rule changes, catching regressions in setups that used to work.
stages.who: deterministic CI running a headless agent

stages.name: AI PR review
stages.what_happens: Claude reviews every PR against REVIEW.md, the team's review SOP written by a human (tech lead). The example sets three passes (bugs, security, compliance), severity tags (important, nit, with a cap on nits) and a do-not-report list (generated files under src/gen). Presenter's tip: let the agent mine human comments on past PRs for recurring patterns and add them to REVIEW.md. A reviewer agent sends comments; a builder agent fixes them in the PR.
stages.who: agent reviewer and agent builder; human writes REVIEW.md
inputs: spec.md and plan.md (per the Anthropic source)
stages.human_gate: Per Anthropic: a person judges intent and risk, a code owner approves, and the authoring agent never approves its own PR. The video only says hooks approve before merge.

stages.name: Guardrail hooks
stages.what_happens: Hooks run deterministic checks on agent actions. They block touching the production database, merging a PR, writing credentials into the codebase, editing protected files, and pushing without formatting or passing tests. Per Anthropic, the release gate is also a hook: dev ships freely, staging asks first, production needs a named person.
stages.human_gate: Production release requires a named human approver (Anthropic source); the agent can take a release up to that gate, never through it.

stages.name: Deploy (before and after release)
stages.what_happens: Before release: a CI workflow calls Claude headless to read a failed build log, find the cause and open a fix PR, which goes through review. After release: Claude checks monitoring tools (Datadog, Sentry). If something breaks, it rolls back with a rollback tool it was given, finds the root cause and opens a PR.
stages.human_gate: PR review and the release gate as above

stages.name: Maintain (close the loop on metrics)
stages.what_happens: A scheduled job (sample YAML covering the past 30 days) has Claude read logs and metrics for repeated errors, slow queries and user churn. Each problem becomes a new intent.md, which restarts the cycle. Per the Anthropic source, detection is a plain script with no AI watching one metric, with three tiers (log, investigate read-only, act through a PR or a pre-approved rollback), and a fixed incident becomes an eval.
inputs: Sentry, Datadog and other metrics and logs
stages.human_gate: People triage the new intent.md (Anthropic source)

pipelines.distinctive: The pipeline is a closed loop held together by an artifact chain of markdown files (intent.md, spec.md, plan.md, REVIEW.md) that is independent of the tracker: the intent can live in git or in any ticket system. Human effort moves from writing to approving at checkpoints. Line-by-line human review is replaced by AI review against the plan plus deterministic hooks as hard gates. The agent setup itself has a regression suite of evals run in CI. Production metrics automatically produce the next intent.
pipelines.caveats: This is a third-party summary video with sponsor segments (Skool community, Johns Hopkins/Great Learning course). It paraphrases loosely and skips the human approval gates the Anthropic source states. Those gates (product owner approves intent and spec, engineer approves plan, code owner approves PR, authoring agent never approves itself, named production approver, three-tier metric detection) were added here from the Anthropic course page and from Dory Zidon's stage-by-stage summary, not from the video. No measurements; all advice is prescriptive. The Anthropic playbook is a vendor guide (self-report). The video date is taken from the task label and was not verified on YouTube.

result.cross_notes: The video and the primary Anthropic material (the Claude Academy course page plus Dory Zidon's stage-by-stage summary of the same playbook) agree on the six stages and on the artifact chain intent.md, spec.md, plan.md, then PR reviewed against REVIEW.md. They also agree on: TDD with a self-check loop (tests, lint, build), 20 to 50 real tasks as evals rerun in CI, hooks as guardrails, and metrics restarting the loop through a new intent.md. Where they differ: the video plays down human gates. The Anthropic version has a named approver at each stage: product owner for intent and spec, engineer for the plan, code owner for the PR, and a named person for production. It also says the authoring agent never approves itself, that plan.md is written in read-only plan mode, that detection is a plain non-AI script with three tiers, and that fixed incidents become evals. The video instead implies AI can review and merge PRs. It also adds things that are not from Anthropic: three test layers (unit, component, e2e), mining past PR comments to build REVIEW.md, and swapping in Matt Pocock or Superpowers skills.

The exact text of Anthropic's intent, spec and plan prompts was not checked against the course lessons
The video's publish date was not checked on YouTube; the date 2026-09 comes from the task label

pipelines.source: IBM Technology (YouTube explainer), "AI in the SDLC: Rethinking AI Coding Tools & AI Agents"

stages.name: Requirements
stages.what_happens: AI synthesizes unstructured inputs (surveys, user reports, emails, stakeholder conversations) to find user-behavior bottlenecks and usage patterns, and generates user stories; production signals (log/bug root-cause analysis) feed back here so requirements reflect what works and fails in production.
stages.who: agent drafts and synthesizes; human product team owns intent
inputs: production logs and bug reports (feedback loop)
stages.human_gate: Implicit: humans own intent and decide which stories become the next features; not described as a formal gate.

stages.name: Design / Spec
stages.what_happens: Spec-driven development: the team's intent is turned into a specification a model can read and follow, and broken into small, well-defined tasks (the explicit cure for 'over-delegation' of big ambiguous asks like 'build me an e-commerce platform' where payments/auth/shipping decisions go unstated).
stages.who: human + agent (human states intent and decisions; agent helps write spec)
stages.human_gate: Humans make the decisions that would otherwise be 'unstated' (payments, auth, shipping, etc.) before handing work to the model.

stages.name: Build (code)
stages.what_happens: The agent harness (agent plus tools around it) takes the spec and fans out to sub-agents: one researches the topic and dependencies, one uses MCP servers to pull data from the team's sources, one edits code to implement features. Shared AGENTS.md-style markdown carries context across teams; skills make outputs consistent whether the model is local, private or cloud.
stages.human_gate: Human role shifts 'from typing to validating'; review of model output is the human check (no specific gate mechanism described).

stages.name: Test
stages.what_happens: AI generates unit tests and test data for specific cases, even directly from a user story, to relieve the manual-testing bottleneck; AI helps diagnose failures from logs and stack traces. Code review by the team is named as the slow step that eats coding gains when output is large.
stages.who: agent generates tests; QA and reviewers (human) validate
stages.human_gate: Team code review (described as the bottleneck when agents produce thousands of unread lines).

stages.name: Release / Deploy
stages.what_happens: Agents write infrastructure as code, e.g. Ansible scripts to update VMs or Kubernetes YAML to deploy containers to hybrid cloud, for stable predictable releases.
stages.who: agent writes IaC; ops (human) runs/owns release
stages.human_gate: Not specified; ops implied as owner.

stages.name: Operate / Maintain
stages.what_happens: Agents analyze logs and bug reports to find root causes (incl. 3 a.m. outages); findings loop back to Requirements/Design. Legacy modernization: AI explains and reverse-engineers code nobody understands to give a path forward.

artifacts.their_name: surveys, user reports, emails, stakeholder conversations

artifacts.role: Unit of intended behavior; also a direct source for generated tests
Machine-readable statement of intent the model follows; prevents unstated decisions
Scope units handed to the agent instead of whole systems
Cross-team context and consistent outputs across models
Generated from stories to unblock QA
Root-cause input that feeds back into requirements

numbers: Cites METR's RCT (July 2025, 'Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity'): developers believed they were ~20% faster but were actually slower; METR's own figure is 19% longer task time, 16 developers, 246 tasks; developers had forecast a 24% speedup (https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study).
Hypothetical: 'coding three times faster' gets absorbed by the other phases, so end-to-end delivery barely changes.
Three example sub-agents in the harness: research, MCP data pull, code editing.
principles: Most SDLC time is waiting between teams (dev waiting on product to clarify a story, ops waiting on dev for a release, QA waiting for a build), across fragmented tools and mismatched environments, not writing code.
Speeding one box (coding) does not speed the whole lifecycle; gains get absorbed elsewhere.
Avoid over-delegation: handing a frontier model a large ambiguous problem hides unstated decisions and produces thousands of unread lines that make review the bottleneck.
Avoid under-delegation: a senior doing all planning and using AI only for snippets keeps 100% of the intellectual heavy lifting human.
Redesign the lifecycle around AI rather than bolting AI onto the existing lifecycle.
Use spec-driven development: give agents small, well-defined tasks from a spec the model can read and follow.
The harness (agent plus tools, sub-agents, MCP, shared markdown context, skills) matters more than the model.
Move the human role from typing to validating and coordinating with other teams.
Feed production signal (logs, bug root causes) back into requirements and design.
Measure outcomes (system health, maintainability and complexity, lead time for changes), not lines of code generated.
pipelines.distinctive: A whole-lifecycle, flow/queue framing: the bottleneck is handoffs and waiting between roles, not coding, so AI is placed at every phase (requirements synthesis, spec, test generation, IaC, ops root-cause) with an explicit operate-to-requirements feedback loop. Frames delegation as a spectrum with two failure ends (over vs under) and spec-driven small tasks as the middle.
pipelines.caveats: Short vendor explainer (IBM Technology) with no described pipeline mechanics: no named tools, gates, artifact states or ticket/PR flow; humans' decision points are implied, not specified. Only external evidence is the METR study, misquoted slightly ('20% less productive'; METR measured 19% longer). Stage list is the classic SDLC (requirements, design, build, test, release, operate), so the 'pipeline' is generic rather than an implemented system. Date taken from task metadata, not verified on YouTube.

result.cross_notes: The video and METR's primary source agree on direction: experienced developers felt faster but were slower with early-2025 AI tools. The speaker says '20% slower'; METR reports 19% longer, with a perceived 20% speedup and a forecast 24% speedup. METR's breakdown (time lost to reviewing AI output, prompting, waiting) supports the video's claim that review becomes the bottleneck.

No concrete human gates, ticket/PR mechanics or numbers for the redesigned pipeline are given.
I did not check the exact publish date on YouTube; 2026-06 comes from the task metadata.
The first search (serper) was rate limited; tavily was used to confirm the METR source.

pipelines.source: Walden Yan (co-founder & CPO, Cognition), talk '40x More Merged PRs With 2.7x the Engineers', AI Engineer conference

stages.name: Intake
stages.what_happens: Customer bug reports, often a video sent in Slack, are forwarded into an internal Slack channel. An engineer tags Devin with a short instruction such as 'please fix this'. Each engineer also keeps a personal Linear board of work items and sends those items to agents.
stages.who: human (a pod engineer who also acts as PM and triager); the customer files the report
inputs: customer bug report (Slack message or video)
Linear ticket on the engineer's own board
stages.human_gate: Light. A human decides what to forward and tags the agent. By default the agents drive the work.

stages.name: Environment provisioning
stages.what_happens: Every agent session starts on a fresh VM snapshot of the latest code. All services run locally under Docker Compose, and every third-party service is mocked, so agents never touch live or staging systems. The snapshots are rebuilt from scratch every hour. When a rebuild fails, Devin fixes it first.
stages.who: deterministic hourly rebuild job, plus the agent (Devin) fixing failed builds
outputs: fresh VM snapshot for each session

stages.name: Implementation
stages.what_happens: Devin implements the change inside the VM and opens a PR.

stages.name: Self-test with evidence
stages.what_happens: The agent tests its own change end to end in the local VM, following testing skills that Devin writes and keeps updated as the codebase changes. Complex setups are tested too, for example several accounts joining one Zoom call inside a single VM. The agent returns a video or recording proving the fix to Slack.
outputs: video or recording proof of the fix
stages.human_gate: Humans mostly review the evidence in Slack instead of the code, often without opening an IDE or GitHub.

stages.name: Automated checks and AI code review
stages.what_happens: CI and lint run, then AI code review. This stage is only mentioned in passing: lint is said to catch bugs 'before they ever hit AI code review'.
stages.who: deterministic CI/lint, then an AI reviewer

stages.name: Merge, monitoring, maintenance
stages.what_happens: PRs go from bug report to merge and then into monitoring and maintenance with no human involved by default. When human judgment is needed, the agent escalates.
stages.who: agent by default; a human only on escalation
outputs: proof sent back to the customer
stages.human_gate: Escalation only: the agent raises the most important decisions to a human, for example at the end of the day.

stages.name: Factory self-improvement (meta-loop)
stages.what_happens: Agents analyse the record of all agent sessions, PRs and decisions to find wasted time or tokens, steps that could become scripts, and missing tests. Every day Devin posts improvement ideas to a Slack channel, such as a Node setup change that saves a minute of CI, or a lint change that catches 20% more bugs before AI review.
inputs: trace of all agent sessions, PRs and decisions
stages.human_gate: Implicit: humans pick which proposals to adopt.

stages.name: Goal-driven 'jobs' (long-running loop)
stages.what_happens: An agent gets a metric goal instead of a task, for example improving P99 latency. It adds telemetry, sets alerts (Datadog), splits the work into tasks, ships PRs, and reports weekly in Slack and daily to the engineer's phone. Two examples were given. In the GPU case the agent had permanently allocated GPUs, tried strategies, and sent the best ones to a human engineer for final approval. In the Android case permanent hooks watch the iOS app and the Slack feedback channels, and the agent keeps parity through live pixel-level QA.
stages.human_gate: Final approval of the strategies found (GPU case). Only the most important decisions are escalated (Android case).

Pods of 2-3 engineers, each owning the full vertical: customer bug reports, QA, product management and engineering

Base review on evidence (videos, recordings) rather than on reading code
Buying an agent is not enough: change the infrastructure so everything runs locally and hermetically, with mocks and no live services
Let agents write and maintain their own testing skills
Run agents over your own agent traces for recursive self-improvement of the factory

Make everything measurable (click latency, layout shift, onboarding retention) and set an agent to optimize each metric 24/7
Teams are limited mainly by their ambition
pipelines.distinctive: Review evidence is videos sent back in Slack instead of human code reading. The local environment is hermetic: Docker Compose plus mocks of every third-party service, rebuilt from scratch every hour, with the agent repairing broken snapshots. An agent-run meta-loop over session traces proposes pipeline improvements every day. Work shifts from per-ticket tasks to long-running, metric-driven jobs that set up their own telemetry, alerts and reports. In one case an agent keeps the Android app in parity with the iOS reference through permanent hooks and pixel-level QA. The org changed too: pods of 2-3 engineers, where each engineer acts as PM, QA and triager for their own board.
pipelines.caveats: This is a vendor talk: Cognition sells Devin, so all numbers are self-reported with no method given. Merged-PR count is a proxy metric, and the quality claim is unsupported. The review and merge gates (who approves merges, branch protection, how AI code review is set up) are not described. No release or deploy stage is described beyond 'merge, monitoring and maintenance'. Specs and plans do not appear as explicit artifacts: tasking is a short Slack message or a Linear item, and goal decomposition happens inside the agent. The source is an auto-generated transcript, so slide content is not visible.

pipelines.source: Derick Chen (AWS, lead of the AI-DLC program in APJ), BuildWithDC YouTube: 'What is AI-DLC? The AI-Driven Development Lifecycle Explained'. Describes AWS's AI-Driven Development Life Cycle (AI-DLC), first published by AWS on the DevOps & Developer Productivity Blog (July 2025, https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/ai-driven-development-life-cycle), with workflow rules open-sourced as awslabs/aidlc-workflows (Nov 2025, per a secondary source; I did not open the repo)

stages.name: Inception 1: Business intent to requirements (Mob Elaboration)
stages.what_happens: The team starts from a business intent or customer pain point (example: customers need to browse and buy products online). The AI breaks it down into full requirements. It analyses the intent and asks clarifying questions (wish list? inventory management? guest checkout or user accounts?). It also flags blind spots early, for example two people buying the last item in stock at the same time.
stages.who: mix: whole team (product owner, devs) plus AI agent; AI proposes and questions, humans answer and validate
stages.human_gate: Team answers the AI's clarifying questions and validates the requirements set (the plan-validate checkpoint of this step)

stages.name: Inception 2: Units of work and roadmap
stages.what_happens: The AI groups user stories into units of work. Each unit is a likely system boundary with high cohesion and loose coupling, small enough for one team to build and run, so several teams can work in parallel. Units are neither huge nor tiny tasks that lose context. The AI also drafts an integration plan and proposes a build order (catalog, then cart, then checkout). It adds complexity-based estimates. A unit can later become a module in a monolith or a microservice.
outputs: implementation roadmap with sequence and estimates
stages.human_gate: Team approves the unit boundaries, sequence and roadmap

stages.name: Construction 1: Domain / conceptual model
stages.what_happens: The team applies domain-driven design, or any other design method it prefers, with the AI. Together they identify entities, value objects and aggregates (product = entity, price = value object, cart = aggregate). The output is business logic placed in domain boundaries. No technology decisions are made in this step.
stages.human_gate: Team validates the domain model; this is where a domain misunderstanding should be caught, before any code exists

stages.name: Construction 2: Logical architecture
stages.what_happens: The conceptual model becomes components, interfaces and integration patterns. The AI suggests architecture choices, for example event-driven inventory updates. Humans weigh the trade-offs and ask the AI for pros and cons. This step settles the compute platform, the databases and the data schema.
stages.who: AI suggests; humans evaluate trade-offs and decide
outputs: logical system architecture with validated, approved decisions (compute, DB, schema)
stages.human_gate: Explicit human approval of each architectural decision after trade-off review

stages.name: Construction 3: Code and tests
stages.what_happens: The AI writes the implementation from the domain model and logical architecture, with all earlier context loaded. It writes automated tests from the inception acceptance criteria. Humans do not review every line. They check that the code matches the strategic intent and validate quality.
stages.human_gate: Quality validation against intent; not line-by-line review

stages.name: Construction 4: Infrastructure as code and non-prod validation
stages.what_happens: The AI writes infrastructure-as-code templates (CloudFormation, Terraform, CDK). It sets up thorough testing in non-production environments. Everything is checked there before production.
stages.who: AI generates IaC; deterministic test runs in non-prod; humans validate
stages.human_gate: Team confirms non-prod validation passed before release

stages.name: Operations 1: Production deployment
stages.what_happens: The validated IaC templates deploy to production. The AI helps set up monitoring and rollback, and can help roll back quickly with the same templates.
stages.who: deterministic IaC deployment; AI assists; humans in control
outputs: live system with monitoring from day one

stages.name: Operations 2: Incident management
stages.what_happens: The AI finds anomalies in metrics and logs and links events to a root cause. It suggests fixes based on similar past incidents. Humans keep control of critical actions: the AI may not restart production services or merge PRs without approval. Follows a you-build-it-you-run-it model.
stages.human_gate: Approval required before restarting production services or merging (landing) PRs

artifacts.role: Shared requirements that every later step and the generated tests refer back to
Loosely coupled slice that one team builds in parallel with others; the unit planning and ownership happen around
Build order, estimates and integration contracts between units
Build cycle of hours to 2-3 days
Components, interfaces, platform, DB, schema decisions
Implementation produced by AI from the approved plan
Operations feedback; PRs need human approval to land

Bolts (build cycles) last no more than 2-3 days vs traditional 2-week sprints
3 phases: Inception (2 steps), Construction (4 steps), Operation (2 steps)

principles: Build context step by step by breaking work down in stages. Do not hand the AI one long prompt or one huge spec it can misread.
Each step's artifacts feed the next step. Trade-off decisions are recorded in the artifacts and the codebase.
Give the AI the right amount of context, not too little and not too much.

Use plan, execute, validate in every step. The AI drafts a plan and asks clarifying questions. Humans verify the plan before execution, so problems are caught while they are cheap and review fatigue drops.
AI does routine implementation; humans own strategic trade-offs and quality validation. Do not micromanage lines of code, and do not give up control.
Validate continuously at every step, not at the end. Fixing in small steps costs far less than fixing at the end.
Make no technology decisions while modelling the domain.
Generate tests from acceptance criteria written in inception
Do not let AI restart production services or merge PRs without human approval
Units of work should be highly cohesive and loosely coupled, sized for one team, so teams can build in parallel.
Whole-team rituals (Mob Elaboration and Mob Construction, named in the AWS blog) replace Scrum ceremonies.
pipelines.distinctive: AI-DLC replaces the SDLC and Scrum with three phases (Inception, Construction, Operation). The AI drives the workflow: it proposes plans and asks questions, and humans validate. Construction refines step by step: technology-free domain model, then logical architecture, then code and tests, then IaC. stages.name: Trigger

result.cross_notes: Agreement: (1) All five start from where people already talk (Slack first; also Linear/GitHub/tickets/cron) and end at a pull request that a human reviews; none auto-merge agent code in the described flows. (2) All run each task in an isolated, pre-warmed, full dev environment (Stripe devbox ~10 s, Ramp Modal snapshot <5 s, Shopify Aquifer sandbox, Brex RDE, Coinbase cached cloud builds), and isolation replaces per-action permission prompts. (3) All reuse human developer infrastructure (CI, linters, rule files/AGENTS.md, skills, MCP tools) and argue 'what is good for humans is good for agents'. (4) All stress closed feedback loops: CI failures, lint, review-bot comments, telemetry and visual evidence fed back to the agent automatically. (5) Human attribution: Ramp opens PRs with the user's token to prevent self-approval; Brex requires agent work be attributed to a real human. (6) Knowledge lives in the repo as rule files/skills/AGENTS.md, scoped and loaded on demand. Disagreements/differences: Stripe is fully unattended with a hard cap of 2 CI rounds and a deterministic-node blueprint; Ramp and Shopify are multiplayer and steerable mid-run; Coinbase moves the human gate earlier (writing a plan/spec as a contract, fix the spec not the code) and tiers review by risk (agent councils for low risk, mandatory humans for money movement); Shopify forbids private use (public channels only) to build a learning corpus. Metrics differ in definition: Stripe 'no human-written code' (1,300+/week), Ramp 'merged PRs written by' (30% Jan -> 74% Oct 2026), Shopify 'coauthored' (1 in 8), Coinbase '75% of PRs created by agents' (vendor story) — not comparable. Common generic pipeline: Work item -> (optional Spec/Plan) -> Sandbox run (agent + deterministic checks) -> Change set (PR) with evidence -> automated checks/review -> human review gate -> merge -> metrics/learning loop.

result.cross_notes: Agreement: (1) All five keep the existing review/merge path and put the agent inside it; the unit of human approval is always the change set (PR / diff / CL) reviewed by the code owner. (2) Deterministic tools do targeting and verification; the LLM does the fuzzy middle (edit generation, propagation decisions, fault invention). Google states this explicitly; Uber AutoClean and Spotify say the same; Airbnb wraps the LLM in a state machine. (3) Fast inner loop of build/test/lint with error feedback is the main quality driver (Spotify verifiers, Airbnb retries, Google ML repair, Uber CI fixers). (4) Added LLM-as-judge or reviewer agents after deterministic checks to catch scope creep and semantic errors (Spotify judge ~25% veto, Uber CodeCourt per-property agents, Meta equivalence detector and judge ensemble, uReview grader). (5) Filter before the human: Uber abandons failing diffs, uReview suppresses low-value categories, Meta reaches out only for ranked catches. (6) Human review capacity is the bottleneck (Google throttled weekly output; Meta moved to human-on-the-loop). Disagreements: Spotify narrows agent tools and wants static prompts with no code search; Uber invests heavily in rich context (Context Graph, 1,000+ MCP tools behind a gateway) for interactive/managed agents. Uber found single end-to-end reviewer agent worse than several single-property reviewers; Spotify uses one judge. Google fine-tunes its own model; others use frontier APIs and keep models swappable. Measurement differs: Google measures end-to-end migration time, Uber measures cost per outcome plus F1/revert rate, Spotify counts merged PRs and estimated time savings, Meta measures acceptance and SEVs prevented. Common shape (tool-agnostic): Work item (from human, chat, or auto-detector) -> Spec/prompt -> Targeting -> Agent edit in sandbox -> Deterministic verify loop -> AI judge/review -> Change set -> CI -> Human owner review -> Merge -> Rollout -> Feedback/evals into prompts and models.

stages.name: PR + AI code review

Code Review runs on every PR before any human: several agents hunt bugs in parallel, a separate vote filters false positives, style-only findings are filtered, rest posted as inline comments marked Important / Nit / Pre-existing. stages.name: Blocking security review + CI

stages.name: Risk-tiered human approval

Sensitive paths (owner-marked, CI workflow files, auth, billing, auto-updater, installers) always require human approval. Trusted repo owners get relaxed requirements; others need a second person. If an agent authored the PR, its operator counts as a required reviewer. Approval is valid for one commit only; untrusted new commits force re-approval. Owners are starting to allow auto-merge of low-risk changes when checks pass.

stages.name: Merge queue / landing

Monorepo (Scion/Antique): a global merge-queue lock could not keep up at 30K merges/day, so they rely on post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing; concurrent changes may conflict and Claude fixes conflicts. stages.human_gate: implicit: flag rollout decisions by owners

Incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the bug; incident-causing PRs become the eval set the reviewer is scored against daily; recurring reviewer findings are fixed at source (skill, lint rule, CLAUDE.md). Review agents also run nightly over existing code.

result.cross_notes:
Agree: (1) The unit of execution is an isolated agent session/sandbox (VM, container, orb) that produces a branch/PR; nobody lets the agent merge by itself. GitHub enforces it hardest (agent cannot mark ready, approve, or merge; requester cannot approve; CI waits for human approval). Linear defers to repo rules. Cognition and Factory keep a human merge but push most checking onto agents. (2) Review is now the bottleneck (Cognition says so outright; Amp and GitHub ship agent reviewers). All four coding vendors run an automated agent review before the human, often with a fix loop. (3) For large work: decompose into fresh-context workers coordinated by an orchestrator (Devin managed sessions, Factory Missions). Both report that context bloat in one session degrades quality. (4) Reusable procedures live in repo or config: Playbooks, Skills, agents.md, .agents/checks, Linear guidance. (5) Well-scoped input matters: Cognition says success scales with specificity, Linear gives an issue-writing guide, Factory treats the planning conversation as the main value.
Disagree / differ: (a) Where the human gate sits. Factory puts it mainly at plan approval, then the human acts as project manager. GitHub and Linear put it at the PR (plus CI approval on GitHub). Cognition keeps the PR gate but filters findings so only escalations reach the human. Amp's is lightest (proof-of-work screenshots; a user pushing to main). (b) Parallelism. Cognition promotes parallel managed Devins; Factory found serial execution with targeted parallelism works better and questions whether broad parallelism helps. (c) The hub of the pipeline. Linear: the work item in the tracker. GitHub: the repo plus permissions, with work arriving as issue or PR. Cognition: the session, reached from many entry points. Factory: the mission plan. Amp: the thread, with no tracker stage. (d) Safety model. GitHub gh-aw is the only one that structurally separates the reasoning job (read-only) from side effects (buffered safe outputs, threat detection, scoped write job). The others rely on sandbox plus human review.
Generic stage skeleton common to all: Work item -> Scoping/Spec -> (Plan approval) -> Decompose -> Implement in sandbox -> Self-verify (tests/QA) -> Agent review + autofix -> Human review -> Merge -> Retrospective/learning (Devin Session Insights, Factory skills).

result.cross_notes: Agreement: (1) Review, not writing, is the new bottleneck (Intercom, Cloudflare, DoorDash, Abnormal, Datadog all say so). (2) Everyone builds in-house harness/platform around an off-the-shelf agent (OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex) for control, context and vendor swap (Cloudflare, DoorDash Flux, Monzo Agent Chip, Abnormal Nora). (3) Company-specific standards/context as a first-class artifact: Cloudflare Codex + AGENTS.md, Intercom skills + review guidance, DoorDash per-domain review profiles. (4) Multi-agent review with decomposition (Intercom sub-agents, Cloudflare coordinator + 7 specialists, DoorDash scout + 2 deep reviewers). (5) Agents run in isolated cloud sandboxes with scoped, audited tool access via an MCP gateway (DoorDash, Monzo, Cloudflare). (6) Generic trigger surfaces: Slack, issue tracker (Linear/Jira), GitHub events, cron. (7) Human escape hatch always exists (break glass, request human review, tag to fix). Disagreements: How far the human gate goes—Intercom lets AI approve and ship ~19% of PRs; Cloudflare says AI review is not a replacement for humans; DoorDash keeps AI review advisory; Abnormal replaces diff-reading with evidence-checking; Datadog replaces review with formal/simulation harnesses for greenfield systems. Review design: DoorDash found specialist fan-out (Cloudflare/Intercom style) misses architectural issues and moved to scout+deep reviewers; Cloudflare keeps specialists with a coordinator judge. Context: DoorDash says AGENTS.md is noisy for review and builds separate review profiles; Cloudflare uses AGENTS.md directly and reviews its freshness. Where design is settled: Abnormal and Cloudflare (spec reviewer) push it before code; Intercom reviews 'problem description vs diff' at PR time. Only Abnormal describes the full issue-to-PR chain (ticket tag -> analysis -> plan with test plan -> PR with evidence); others describe mostly the PR/review segment.

stages.name: Intent / User Request
stages.what_happens: A human states a high-level problem ('Using AI-DLC let's build...' or '/aidlc <intent>'). The workflow picks a profile for it.

stages.name: Inception: Workspace Detection
stages.what_happens: AI checks whether the project is greenfield or brownfield and creates the aidlc-docs folder that holds every artifact.

stages.name: Inception: Reverse Engineering (conditional, brownfield only)
stages.what_happens: AI documents the existing codebase before requirements work starts.

stages.name: Inception: Requirements Analysis (Mob Elaboration)
stages.what_happens: AI writes multiple-choice clarifying questions, each with an 'Other' option, into a file. Humans answer inline. AI flags contradictions or ambiguities, then writes requirements.md.
stages.human_gate: Team answers the questions, then chooses Approve & Continue / Request Changes

stages.name: Inception: User Stories, Application Design, Units Generation (conditional)
stages.what_happens: AI breaks the requirements into stories and Units of Work (which replace epics), proposes an architecture, and recommends which of these stages to skip.
stages.human_gate: Approve, or override AI's decision to skip a stage

stages.name: Inception: Workflow Planning
stages.what_happens: AI writes an execution plan that lists which stages will run and which are skipped, with a risk assessment.
stages.human_gate: Approve the plan or add back skipped stages

stages.name: Construction: Functional Design, NFR Requirements, NFR Design, Infrastructure Design (conditional, per unit; Mob Construction)
stages.what_happens: AI proposes the domain model, non-functional requirements and their design, and the infrastructure. The team settles technical decisions in real time.
stages.human_gate: Team validates the architecture and technical choices

stages.name: Construction: Code Generation Planning
stages.what_happens: AI writes a numbered checkbox plan per unit covering business logic, API, data layer, tests, docs and deployment files.
stages.human_gate: Approve the plan or request changes

stages.name: Construction: Code Generation
stages.what_happens: AI carries out the plan step by step, ticks the checkboxes and keeps traceability back to the stories.

stages.name: Construction: Build and Test (repeats for each unit)
stages.what_happens: AI writes build and test instructions (unit, integration, performance, security/contract/e2e) and a summary of whether the project is ready to deploy.

stages.name: Operations
stages.what_happens: AI uses the context gathered so far to manage infrastructure as code, deployment and monitoring, with the team overseeing it.
stages.human_gate: Approval for production deployments, permission changes and destructive actions

stages.name: Ticket / task

stages.name: Questions (QRSPI addition)

stages.what_happens: Agent dumps its understanding into an artifact of about 200 lines: current state, desired end state, design decisions, open questions. The human does 'brain surgery', for example redirecting it away from legacy patterns.

stages.name: Structure outline (QRSPI)
stages.what_happens: Like a C header file: signatures, new types and phases as vertical slices with checkpoints.

stages.name: Plan
stages.what_happens: Exact steps, the files to edit and how, and the testing and verification for each phase.
stages.human_gate: In RPI this is the main review ('I can read 200 lines of plan, not 2000 lines of Go'). In QRSPI it is a spot-check only

stages.name: Worktree
stages.what_happens: Work is isolated in a git worktree. This is the only step that needs one; everything else happens on main.

stages.name: Implement
stages.what_happens: Agent goes through the plan phase by phase with a fresh context each phase. After each verified phase it compacts status back into the plan. One commit per phase.

stages.name: PR / code review
stages.what_happens: Humans review the code. Horthy: engineers must read and own the code. In 2025 he said he reads the tests carefully and relies on specs for the rest.

pipelines.source: Kent Beck: 'Augmented Coding: Beyond the Vibes' (B+ tree, BPlusTree3)

stages.name: Write plan.md as a test list
stages.what_happens: Human keeps plan.md as an ordered list of tests to write, each marked when done.
stages.human_gate: Human owns the test list and the design

stages.name: 'go': Red
stages.what_happens: Agent finds the next unmarked test in plan.md and writes the simplest failing test.
stages.human_gate: Human watches intermediate results and may say 'for the next test add keys in reverse order'

stages.name: Green
stages.what_happens: Agent writes only enough code to pass that test and runs all tests except long-running ones.
stages.human_gate: Human intervenes on warning signs: loops, unrequested functionality, cheating such as disabling or deleting tests

stages.name: Refactor / Tidy First
stages.what_happens: Structural changes (rename, extract, move) are kept separate from behavioural changes, and structural ones go first. Tests run before and after.

stages.name: Commit
stages.what_happens: Commit only when all tests pass and there are no warnings. One logical unit per commit, labelled as structural or behavioural.

stages.name: Restart / re-scope when stuck
stages.what_happens: When complexity stalled the genie, the human threw away versions 1 and 2, and transliterated a working Python version into Rust using a remote agent.
stages.human_gate: Human decides to restart or switch strategy

numbers: About 4 weeks of part-time work; one day was 13 hours
Third attempt (BPlusTree3); the first 2 stalled under accumulated complexity
Result: slightly slower than Rust BTreeMap / Python SortedDict on some operations, faster at range scans
principles: Augmented coding cares about the code, its complexity, tests and coverage; vibe coding cares only about behaviour
TDD red, green, refactor, one test at a time
Never mix structural and behavioural changes in a commit
Watch for loops, unrequested features and test cheating, and stop them
Intrude on design to keep the genie from coding ahead
Humans make more consequential decisions per hour and fewer vanilla ones
pipelines.distinctive: A single developer and a single agent in a very tight inner loop. The unit of work is one test. The 'plan' is a TDD test list, and the human gate is continuous observation, not phase approvals.
pipelines.caveats: One person, one library project. No team process, issues or PRs. He admits the code quality is still not good enough for him because of accidental complexity.

pipelines.source: Simon Willison: 'Agentic Engineering Patterns' guide

stages.name: Explore options / prototype
stages.what_happens: Agents list options and build cheap throwaway prototypes or load tests to prove a technology choice. 'Hoard things you know how to do' gives working examples to recombine.

stages.name: Start session: first run the tests
stages.what_happens: Agent runs the existing test suite first, to learn the project and the test harness.

stages.name: Implement with red/green TDD
stages.what_happens: Write tests, confirm they fail, then implement until they pass. Async agents (Codex web, Jules, Claude Code web) can do refactors in a branch or worktree.

stages.name: Agentic manual testing
stages.what_happens: Agent exercises the code (python -c, curl, Playwright/Rodney with screenshots) and records evidence with Showboat (note/exec/image). Bugs it finds get fixed with red/green TDD so they become permanent tests.

stages.name: Understand the code (linear walkthrough)
stages.what_happens: Agent produces a linear walkthrough or interactive explanation so the human understands what was built.

stages.name: Self-review before PR
stages.what_happens: The author confirms the code works and reviews the PR description too.
outputs: small PR with context + evidence (manual test notes, screenshots, video)
stages.human_gate: Author must have reviewed it; 'don't file PRs with code you haven't reviewed yourself'

stages.name: Evaluate PR
stages.what_happens: Land it if good, prompt again if almost there, throw it away if bad.

stages.name: Compound step
stages.what_happens: Retrospective after each project: document what worked into the agent instructions for future runs (credited to Every's Compound Engineering).

artifacts.role: Proof of what was run and its output

principles: Writing code is cheap now, but good code still has a cost
Never assume LLM code works until it has been executed
Use red/green TDD and confirm the tests fail first
Passing tests is not proof; also have the agent test 'manually' and show its work
Don't inflict unreviewed code on collaborators: small PRs, context, evidence
Shipping worse code with agents is a choice. Use agents to pay down tech debt (zero tolerance for minor smells)
Embrace the compound engineering loop
Sub-agents for exploration and parallel or specialist work
pipelines.distinctive: Puts verification evidence first: an agent-produced proof-of-testing document (Showboat) attached to the PR, plus agent-written walkthroughs so the human understands the code. The responsibility for the first review stays with the PR author.
pipelines.caveats: A collection of patterns, not a single enforced pipeline. I assembled the order from the chapters. Oriented to an individual engineer and OSS. No numbers.

pipelines.source: Steve Yegge: 'Welcome to Gas Town' (multi-agent orchestrator on Beads)

stages.name: Plan / design (feed the engine)
stages.what_happens: The human, acting as 'Product Manager', designs features and implementation plans, possibly with Spec Kit or BMAD. An agent then converts the plan into Beads epics.
stages.who: human (Overseer) + Crew agents for design back-and-forth
stages.human_gate: Human decides what to build; polecat work should be 'decomposed and vetted multiple times'

stages.name: File & sling
stages.what_happens: The Mayor files a bead and runs `gt sling` to put it on a worker's hook. Work is wrapped in a Convoy, the tracked delivery unit.
stages.human_gate: Human tells the Mayor what to sling

stages.name: Execute (Polecats swarm)
stages.what_happens: Ephemeral Polecat workers pick up the hooked work, one per worktree, and follow a molecule (a chained workflow of beads such as design, plan, implement, review, test). Formulas like 'Rule of Five' add review passes. GUPP rule: if there is work on your hook, you must run it.

stages.name: Supervise
stages.what_happens: Witness patrols the polecats and refinery and unsticks them. Deacon plus a daemon heartbeat keep the town running. Dogs do maintenance.

stages.name: Merge Queue (Refinery)
stages.what_happens: Refinery agent merges MRs one at a time into main, re-imagining changes when the baseline has moved. No work is lost; it can escalate.
stages.human_gate: none by default; optional manual merge by the Mayor or human

stages.name: Convoy lands
stages.what_happens: The Mayor is notified that the convoy finished and the human reviews dashboards and activity feeds.
stages.human_gate: Human picks a winner among duplicate fixes and redoes lost designs

artifacts.generic_name: Work item (issue in a git-backed tracker)
artifacts.role: Atomic unit of work; also mail, identities and hooks
Durable, step-by-step workflows that survive crashes
Tracks a batch of work to completion
Orchestration steps not persisted to git

numbers: 20-30 agents in parallel, productively and sustained; usually about 12 active
Gas Town (Go): 17 days, 75k LOC, 2000 commits; 4th orchestrator in 2025
Beads: about 225k LOC of Go, never read by the author
Requires multiple Claude accounts; 'expensive as hell'
Agents nudged within 30-60s of startup and at most about 5 min later; Boot dog woken every 5 min
Rule of Five: each step reviewed 5 times with different focus
principles: Agent is not a session: identities and work persist in git (Beads); sessions are cattle
GUPP: if there is work on your hook, you must run it
Nondeterministic idempotence: the path varies but the workflow eventually completes
Polecats get well-specified work and shouldn't have to make decisions
Throughput over efficiency: some work is lost or duplicated and that's accepted
The human is the Product Manager; the hard problem is keeping the engine fed with plans
Only for people at 'Stage 7+' (10+ agents hand-managed)
pipelines.distinctive: An industrial-scale factory: a persistent work graph (Beads issue tracker in git) is the control plane, with role-specialised agents (Mayor, Polecats, Refinery merge-queue agent, Witness, Deacon) and an agent-run merge queue. Human review of code is mostly absent; the human gate is upstream (planning) and downstream (picking winners).
pipelines.caveats: Explicitly '100% vibe coded', the author has never seen the code, it was 3 weeks old at the time of writing, and he says 'do not use Gas Town'. Self-report only; no quality metrics. Built for the author's own projects.

pipelines.source: Geoffrey Huntley: 'Ralph Wiggum as a software engineer' (Ralph loop)

stages.name: Spec conversation
stages.what_happens: A long conversation with the LLM about requirements, then a prompt to write the specs out one per file in specs/.
stages.human_gate: Human shapes the specs (a wrong spec was the costliest error: a lexer keyword defined twice went unnoticed for a month)

stages.name: Planning loop
stages.what_happens: A separate prompt has up to 500 sub-agents compare src/ against specs/, search for TODOs, placeholders and minimal implementations, and write fix_plan.md as a priority-sorted bullet list.
stages.human_gate: Human watches the TODO list 'like a hawk' and often deletes and regenerates it

stages.name: Building loop: `while :; do cat PROMPT.md | agent; done`
stages.what_happens: Each iteration gets a fresh context with the same stack (specs + fix_plan.md + AGENT.md). The agent picks the single most important item, searches before assuming something is unimplemented, and implements it using sub-agents. Only 1 sub-agent runs build/test.

stages.name: Back-pressure
stages.what_happens: Tests for the changed unit, type checker, static analysers and security scanners reject bad output. Tests record why they exist, as notes for future loops.

stages.name: Commit, push, tag
stages.what_happens: When tests pass: update fix_plan.md, `git add -A`, commit, push. Tag a version when there are no build or test errors. Learnings go into AGENT.md.

stages.name: Tune Ralph
stages.what_happens: Human watches the stream for bad behaviour and adds 'signs' to the prompt. On a broken codebase, chooses between `git reset --hard` plus restart, or rescue prompts.
stages.human_gate: Human judgment call on reset vs rescue

artifacts.role: Requirements, one file per topic, loaded every loop

artifacts.generic_name: Backlog / plan (work items as a priority list)

artifacts.role: How to build and test; self-improved by the agent

numbers: About 170k usable context window; one item per loop
Up to 500 parallel sub-agents for search/write, 1 for build/test
'Expect to get 90% done' on greenfield
Repomirror hackathon: 6 repos shipped overnight (linked anecdote)
principles: Monolithic: one process, one repo, one task per loop. Multi-agent is not needed yet
Deterministically allocate the same context stack each loop (specs + plan)
Main context is a scheduler; push expensive work to sub-agents
Don't assume it's not implemented; search first
Back-pressure must be fast: the speed of the wheel matters
No placeholder implementations
Loop back is everything: let the agent evaluate its own output
Engineers are still needed; senior expertise guides Ralph
'There's no way in heck would I use Ralph in an existing code base'
pipelines.distinctive: The simplest possible orchestrator, a bash while-loop with a fresh context per iteration. State lives only in files (specs, fix_plan, AGENT.md). There are no PRs or human code review; quality comes from deterministic back-pressure plus prompt tuning.
pipelines.caveats: Greenfield only, by the author's own account. It produces a broken codebase at times and the repo 'full of garbage'. Maintainability is explicitly dismissed. Evidence is a single project (the CURSED language).

pipelines.source: Addy Osmani (Google): 'My LLM coding workflow going into 2026' + 'How to write a good spec for AI agents'

stages.name: Spec ('15-minute waterfall')
stages.what_happens: Brainstorm with the AI, which asks questions until the requirements and edge cases are clear. The result is compiled into spec.md: requirements, architecture decisions, data models, testing strategy. Plan Mode (read-only) can be used.
stages.human_gate: Human confirms the spec captures what they want

stages.name: Plan
stages.what_happens: A reasoning model breaks the spec into bite-sized tasks or milestones. It is iterated and critiqued until coherent, and may be stored as a 'prompt plan' file.

stages.name: Context packing
stages.what_happens: Load relevant code, docs and constraints (CLAUDE.md/GEMINI.md rules, Context7, gitingest, Skills).

stages.name: Implement one chunk
stages.what_happens: 'Implement step 1 from the plan'. One function or feature at a time, optionally in parallel worktrees or async agents (Jules, Copilot Agent) that open PRs.

stages.name: Test + automated gates
stages.what_happens: Agent runs the tests and fixes failures. CI, linters and type checkers run, and their output goes back to the agent. Chrome DevTools MCP is used for runtime checks.

stages.name: Review
stages.what_happens: Human reviews line by line. A second model or AI reviewer (e.g. CodeRabbit) critiques. Review depth scales with scope.
stages.human_gate: 'Never commit code you can't explain'; merge only after understanding

stages.name: Commit (save point)
stages.what_happens: Granular commit after each chunk; branches and worktrees isolate experiments.

numbers: Cites about 90% of Claude Code's code being written by Claude Code (Anthropic claim, not his measurement)
Some engineers run 3-4 agents in parallel; he mostly uses 1 main agent + 1 reviewer
principles: Specs before code
Small iterative chunks; avoid huge leaps
Provide extensive context
Use the right model and switch when stuck
Human in the loop: treat AI as an over-confident junior; test and review everything
Commit often; never commit code you can't explain
Strong CI, linters and tests are force multipliers; AI-on-AI review
AI amplifies existing skills, good or bad
pipelines.distinctive: A mainstream, conservative 'AI-assisted engineering' synthesis: classic SE discipline (design doc, small tasks, CI, review, commits) applied to a supervised agent. Review depth scales with how much is delegated.
pipelines.caveats: Individual workflow, opinion-based, no measured outcomes. Author works on Gemini at Google (disclosed). Little detail on team-level artifacts such as issues or tickets.

result.cross_notes:
The sources agree on these points:
(1) Intent is written down before code (spec, research or plan). AI-DLC, the SDD tools, RPI/QRSPI, Ralph (specs/), Osmani (spec.md) and Beck (plan.md as a test list) all do it.
(2) State lives in files or a tracker, not in the chat session. Examples: aidlc-docs and audit.md, research/plan.md, fix_plan.md and AGENT.md, Beads in git. A fresh context per phase or iteration is the norm (HumanLayer, Ralph, Gas Town, AI-DLC's on-demand rule loading).
(3) Deterministic back-pressure (tests, type checkers, CI, linters) is the core verification layer. TDD in particular: Beck, Willison red/green, Ralph, Osmani.
(4) Work is cut into small units (one test, one chunk, one item per loop, one unit of work, one bead).
(5) A project-memory layer is separate from the per-change spec: steering, constitution, CLAUDE.md, AGENT.md, compound step.

They disagree on these points:
(a) Where the human gate sits.
- Upstream on research and design (HumanLayer: 'a bad line of research = thousands of bad lines of code'; AI-DLC: approval at every stage, done as a mob).
- Continuously in the inner loop (Beck watches every test).
- At the PR (Willison and Osmani: the author must review and explain the code).
- Almost none on code (Ralph and Gas Town: the human tunes prompts and feeds plans; agents merge directly or via an agent merge queue).
(b) How much ceremony.
- AI-DLC and spec-kit are heavy. Böckeler criticises this as 'Verschlimmbesserung', with Kiro turning one bug into 16 acceptance criteria.
- AWS and HumanLayer both later moved to adaptive or variable depth (AI-DLC Principle 10; QRSPI is still 8 steps, and Horthy says not every task needs all of them).
(c) Single agent or swarm.
- Huntley: monolith, multi-agent not needed.
- Yegge: 20-30 agents with roles.
- Horthy: sub-agents are for context control, not personas.
(d) Whether specs replace code review. Horthy (2025) let go of reading every line but kept reading the tests. By 2026 he insists engineers read and own the code. Böckeler would rather review code than markdown.
(e) Greenfield vs brownfield. Ralph is greenfield only. HumanLayer targets 300k LOC brownfield. AI-DLC branches on it (Reverse Engineering stage).

A tool-agnostic chain common to most of them: Work item (ticket/issue/bead/intent) -> Clarification questions -> Research/codebase map -> Spec/requirements -> Design -> Plan/task list -> Isolated change set (branch/worktree) -> Implement + automated checks (tests/CI) -> Verification evidence -> Review (PR/MR) -> Merge (human or merge queue) -> Release/Operate -> Learnings written back into project memory/rules.

stages.name: Spec by interview
stages.what_happens: When the requirement is fuzzy, Claude interviews the human with multiple-choice questions until it can write a spec file.
stages.human_gate: Human answers questions and decides scope, which only they know ('be ambitious' or not)

stages.name: Build in a fresh session
stages.what_happens: New clean-context session implements from SPEC.md. Uses CLAUDE.md (commands, gotchas, team decisions), skills (team procedures), MCP/CLI (issue tracker, gh). Parallel work goes in separate git worktrees.
stages.human_gate: Watch the first minute, Esc to redirect; after two failed corrections /clear and rewrite the prompt

stages.name: Self-check loop
stages.what_happens: Agent runs a pass/fail check (tests, typecheck, lint, fixture diff, screenshot vs mockup) and iterates until green. Can be enforced deterministically by a Stop hook (exit 2 blocks finishing) or by /goal (a separate model checks the condition after every turn).
stages.human_gate: none (automated); human asks for evidence, not 'all tests pass'

stages.name: Independent review against spec
stages.what_happens: A fresh subagent that never saw the writing conversation (/code-review, or a read-only 'reviewer' agent with tools Read/Grep/Glob) compares the diff to SPEC.md, reports only correctness gaps, skips style. Findings fed back to the builder.
stages.human_gate: none; human decides which findings to fix (fixing every finding over-engineers)

stages.name: Verify running app
stages.what_happens: /verify builds and runs the app and looks at the result to catch what tests miss.

stages.name: Hand-off and sign-off
stages.what_happens: Result lands as a PR, comment or summary; a person approves merge/deploy. Branch protection is the deterministic last word.
stages.human_gate: Person approves the merge, the deploy, or anything irreversible

artifacts.role: Written definition of done; input to build and to review
What the agent cannot find in the code: commands, gotchas, team procedures
Deterministic rules that must never/always happen

numbers: CLAUDE.md recommended under 200 lines
Stop hook: after 8 consecutive blocked stops Claude Code overrides the next block
Auto mode pauses after 3 blocks in a row or 20 total
/batch splits a big mechanical change into 5 to 30 units, each in its own worktree and PR
Prompt cache ~1 hour on subscription, 5 minutes on API key
principles: Split instructions into non-deterministic (prompt, CLAUDE.md, skills: model decides) and deterministic (hooks, deny rules, CI, branch protection: harness enforces); rules with zero exceptions go to the deterministic side
Give the agent a check that returns pass/fail; otherwise you are the test suite
Ask for evidence, not claims
Reviewer must not have seen the writing; review against the spec and skip style
Only write down what the agent cannot find in the repo
Before unattended runs answer five questions: what is done, how does it check itself, what may it touch, what stops it (max turns/budget), where does the result go and who signs off
The human keeps three things: starting the run, defining done, approving the merge
pipelines.distinctive: Explicit table mapping each concern (what to do, what it can touch, when it is done, spend, last word) to a soft vs hard control; spec written via agent interview and then built in a fresh session; reviewer as a separate tool-restricted agent.
pipelines.caveats: Vendor guidance for its own tool; no measured outcomes; workflow is per-developer, not a team process; issue tracker treated as an external context source only.

result.cross_notes:
The sources agree on a common core: work item -> (optional spec/interview) -> plan reviewed by a human before code -> agent implements in an isolated environment (worktree, cloud VM, Actions runner) guided by a repo instruction file (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / copilot-instructions.md; Jules, Copilot and Codex all read AGENTS.md) -> agent runs tests/lint itself and iterates -> independent review (separate agent and/or human) -> PR -> human approves merge under branch protection/CI. All of them put the irreversible decision (merge/deploy) with a human. Everyone says: give the agent a runnable check, keep tasks well-scoped (OpenAI: ~1 hour / few hundred lines; GitHub: clear acceptance criteria and file hints), and pre-configure the environment. Every source treats the PR as the unit of human review.
Differences: (1) Where the work item lives. GitHub and Jules are issue-tracker-native (issue = prompt, assigning or labeling starts the run). Anthropic and OpenAI treat the tracker as external context via CLI/MCP, and the unit is a prompt or SPEC.md. Antigravity has no tracker or PR stage, only artifacts in the IDE. Microsoft adds an operations loop (SRE agent opens issues from incidents). (2) How strong the plan gate is. It is mandatory in Jules and in Antigravity's plan review. It is recommended for complex tasks in Codex, GitHub and Anthropic. (3) Who reviews. Anthropic stresses a reviewer with fresh context that checks against the spec and skips style. OpenAI and Microsoft run AI review on 100% / 90% of PRs. GitHub's agent review is a Comment, not an Approve, by default. (4) Enforcement. Anthropic explicitly separates soft instructions from deterministic hooks, deny rules and branch protection. The others mention it only lightly (GitHub hooks, Codex sandbox/approval). (5) Codifying lessons. Codex has a clear ladder: prompt -> AGENTS.md -> skill -> scheduled task. Anthropic and GitHub have similar pieces (skills, custom agents, automations). (6) DORA is the only measured source. It warns that AI raises throughput but hurts stability unless batches are small, tests are automated and version control is strong. The vendors' fast-parallel-PR advice is in tension with this, so a pipeline needs a small-batch rule plus a review-capacity gate. Self-reported vendor numbers (Microsoft 88% throughput, Anthropic 70-80% agent share) have no method behind them.

standards.name: CDEvents (CD Foundation), spec v0.5.0 docs; main branch started v0.6 on 2025-12-22
standards.what: Tool-neutral event vocabulary for CI/CD built on CloudEvents. Every event is subject + predicate (e.g. dev.cdevents.change.merged.0.3.0). The events are declarative: they state what happened and do not command anything. Subjects are either long-running (service, environment, artifact, change) or run-to-completion (taskRun, build, test). The spec says change.created covers a GitHub PullRequest, a GitLab MergeRequest and a Gerrit Change. Artifacts are identified by purl. The primer says the events give enough data for 2 DORA metrics (lead time, deployment frequency).
vocabulary: Ops: incident (detected/reported/resolved), ticket (created/updated/closed); ticketType bug/enhancement/incident/task/question; resolution completed/withdrawn/duplicate
Context: id, source, type, timestamp, chainId, links (PATH/RELATION TRIGGER/END) for end-to-end correlation

standards.name: CDF SIG Interoperability tool terminology (cited in CDEvents primer and 2022 whitepaper)
standards.what: A cross-tool table of CI/CD terms. The 2022 whitepaper uses 'pipeline' for pipeline/workflow and 'task' for job/stage/step. The CDF blog table maps each tool's terms: GitHub Actions Step/Job/Workflow/Event/Runner, GitLab Job/Stage/Pipeline/Trigger/Runner, Tekton Step/Task/Pipeline, Jenkins Job/Stage/Pipeline/Agent.

standards.name: OpenTelemetry CI/CD + VCS semantic conventions (Release Candidate)
standards.what: Standard attribute names for telemetry about pipelines and version control. vcs.change is defined as a pull request, merge request or changelist. GitHub issue #915 proposed reusing CDEvents subjects as the subject types.

standards.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI agent spans (Development status, 2025-2026)
standards.what: Draft conventions for telemetry from agent runs. invoke_agent is for an LLM-driven loop and invoke_workflow is for app-defined control flow. The draft also defines a plan span and an execute_tool span.

standards.name: SLSA Provenance v1 (v1.1 page; v1.2 is current)
standards.what: An in-toto attestation that a given build platform produced a given set of artifacts, identified by digest, from a given set of inputs. This is the standard 'how was this artifact made' record. SLSA also defines a Verification Summary Attestation, which records a verifier's pass/fail decision.
vocabulary: runDetails (builder.id, invocationId, startedOn/finishedOn, byproducts e.g. logs)

standards.name: Flow Framework (Mik Kersten, Project to Product; Planview)
standards.what: Sorts all delivery work into 4 mutually exclusive flow item types and measures flow across the tool network. Its 'Artifact Network' layer maps tool records (issues, PRs, builds) onto the flow items. This makes it the closest standard to a tool-agnostic 'work item' type.
vocabulary: Flow items: Feature (business value), Defect (quality), Risk (security/compliance), Debt (impediments to future delivery)
Flow metrics: velocity, time, load, efficiency, distribution
Model layers: Tool Network, Artifact Network, Value Stream Network; activity model Ideate/Create/Release/Operate

standards.name: GitLab Value Stream Analytics (docs, current)
standards.what: A vendor implementation of value stream management. A stage is a pair of start and end events on an issue or merge request. The default stages show how one tool links work items to changes.
vocabulary: Default stages: Issue, Plan, Code, Test, Review, Staging
Events: issue created/first assigned/first mentioned in commit/closed; MR created/first committed/reviewer assigned/last approved/last build started-finished/merged/first deployed to production
Lead time (issue created to closed), cycle time (first commit reference to issue closed)
Linkage: 'Closes #123' pattern ties a change to a work item

standards.name: DORA software delivery performance metrics (guide updated 2026-01-05)
standards.what: Defines the delivery outcome nouns that matter: change, deployment, failed deployment, recovery. It now has five metrics. MTTR has been replaced by failed deployment recovery time, and deployment rework rate is new.
vocabulary: Change lead time: committed to version control -> deployed in production
Change fail rate: deployments requiring immediate intervention (rollback/hotfix)
Deployment rework rate: unplanned deployments caused by a production incident

standards.name: ITIL 4 (change enablement, incident, problem, service request)
standards.what: The ITSM vocabulary for operations-side nouns. These definitions come from secondary glossaries; the AXELOS primary text is paywalled and was not read.
vocabulary: Change: addition, modification or removal of anything that could affect IT services (standard / normal / emergency)
Incident: unplanned interruption or reduction in quality of a service
Problem: cause or potential cause of one or more incidents
Service request: a user request for information, a standard change or a service

standards.name: A2A (Agent2Agent) protocol specification, v1.0 line
standards.what: Standard object model for delegating work to an agent. The Task is the stateful unit of work, with a lifecycle and outputs called artifacts. contextId groups related tasks and messages into one session or conversation.
vocabulary: TaskState: submitted, working, input_required, auth_required, completed, failed, canceled, rejected
Artifact = task output composed of Parts

standards.name: Agent Trace (Cursor), v0.1.0 RFC, January 2026
standards.what: Vendor-neutral JSON 'trace record' that ties code ranges in a VCS revision to the agent conversation and model that produced them. It does not prescribe storage (files, git notes or a database) and works with Git, jj, Mercurial and SVN. This is the first spec for attributing code to an agent session.
vocabulary: contributor type: human / ai / mixed / unknown

standards.name: Atlassian Jira terminology (support KB, updated 2025-10-27)

proposed_vocabulary.definition: Any raw input that might become work and is not yet accepted: an alert, error spike, user feedback, a CVE, a request, an idea. It is triaged into a Work item or dropped.

proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: CDEvents incident.detected (for operational signals); ITIL event / service request; GitLab VSA 'Issue created'

proposed_vocabulary.definition: The unit of accepted, tracked work, with one owner, a state and a type: feature, defect, risk or debt. Everything downstream links back to it.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: GitHub Issue, Jira work item (formerly 'issue'), Linear issue, GitLab issue, Azure Boards work item
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: CDEvents ticket (created/updated/closed, ticketType); Flow Framework flow item (Feature/Defect/Risk/Debt); A2A Task when delegated to an agent

proposed_vocabulary.definition: The written statement of what 'done' means for a work item: intent, acceptance criteria, constraints. A reviewer or verifier judges the result against it.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: Issue body with acceptance criteria, PRD/RFC doc (Notion, Google Docs), ADR file in repo, Linear project doc, spec.md in an agent workflow

proposed_vocabulary.definition: How the work item will be done, broken into ordered steps or sub-items. It is written before code is produced and can be revised.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: Jira/Linear/GitHub sub-issues and sub-tasks, checklist in the issue, agent plan file or plan mode output
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: OpenTelemetry GenAI 'plan' span (development); Jira parent/child hierarchy

proposed_vocabulary.definition: One execution of a human or agent working on a work item. It has inputs, a transcript, tool calls, cost and a final state (completed/failed/needs input), and it produces change sets and reports.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: Claude Code / Codex / Copilot coding agent session, Devin session, Cursor background agent run
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: A2A Task + contextId + TaskState; OpenTelemetry invoke_agent / invoke_workflow span; Agent Trace 'conversation'

proposed_vocabulary.definition: A proposed, reviewable modification to a repository: one or more commits on a ref, targeting a base ref, linked to its work item. It is merged or abandoned.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: GitHub pull request, GitLab merge request, Gerrit change, Phabricator diff, jj change, Bitbucket PR
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: CDEvents change (created/updated/reviewed/merged/abandoned) + branch + repository; OpenTelemetry vcs.change / vcs.ref; ITIL change (broader: any modification affecting a service)

proposed_vocabulary.definition: One execution of an automated workflow (build, test, scan, deploy) triggered by an event such as a push, a change set update, a tag or a schedule. It is made of task runs.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: GitHub Actions workflow run/job/step, GitLab pipeline/job, Jenkins build, Buildkite build, Tekton PipelineRun/TaskRun, CircleCI workflow
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: CDEvents pipelineRun / taskRun / build; OpenTelemetry cicd.pipeline.run, cicd.pipeline.task.run

proposed_vocabulary.definition: The machine-readable outcome of one automated check against a change set or artifact: pass/fail/skip, plus details such as tests, lint, type check, security scan or coverage.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: GitHub check run / commit status, GitLab job status + test report, JUnit XML, SonarQube quality gate, Snyk/CodeQL findings
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: CDEvents testCaseRun / testSuiteRun finished (outcome), testOutput; OpenTelemetry cicd.pipeline.result

proposed_vocabulary.definition: A judgement on a change set by a person or an agent: approve, request changes or comment, with findings tied to lines. It differs from a check result because a person or agent made the judgement, not a script.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: GitHub PR review, GitLab approval + discussions, Gerrit Code-Review vote, AI reviewer comments (CodeRabbit, Copilot review)

proposed_vocabulary.definition: The single go/no-go decision that combines the check results, reviews and policy for one transition: merge, release or promote. It names who or what decided and on what evidence.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: Branch protection / required checks, merge queue result, GitLab approval rules, Argo Rollouts analysis result, change approval board sign-off, deployment protection rules
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: SLSA Verification Summary Attestation (pass/fail by a verifier); ITIL change authorization; no CDEvents subject (closest is change.merged)

proposed_vocabulary.definition: An immutable output of a pipeline run, identified by content digest. It is what actually ships, and it carries provenance: which source revision, builder and inputs produced it.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: OCI/Docker image, npm/PyPI/Maven package, binary, mobile app bundle, GitHub release asset, Artifactory item
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: CDEvents artifact (packaged/signed/published, purl id); SLSA provenance subject + buildDefinition/runDetails; in-toto attestation

proposed_vocabulary.definition: A named, versioned selection of artifacts declared ready to ship, with notes on which change sets and work items it contains. It can exist before or without deployment, e.g. a library.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: Git tag + GitHub Release, GitLab release, changelog entry, App Store version, semantic-release output
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: No dedicated CDEvents subject (closest: artifact.published); SemVer; Flow Framework 'Release' activity

proposed_vocabulary.definition: Putting a specific artifact version into a specific environment, recorded with its outcome (succeeded, rolled back). This is the event DORA counts.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: Argo CD sync, Flux reconciliation, GitHub deployment/environment, GitLab environment deployment, Kubernetes rollout, Vercel/Netlify deploy, Dokploy deploy
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: CDEvents service.deployed/upgraded/rolledback/removed + environment; DORA deployment (frequency, change fail rate, rework rate); ITIL change (implemented)

proposed_vocabulary.definition: A confirmed unplanned interruption or quality drop in a running service. It is linked to the deployment or change that likely caused it and to the follow-up work items it creates.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: PagerDuty / Opsgenie incident, Jira Service Management incident, incident.io, Sentry issue escalated, status page entry
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: CDEvents incident (detected/reported/resolved); ITIL incident (and problem = root cause); DORA failed deployment / recovery time

proposed_vocabulary.definition: A human-readable account of what happened, closing a loop: run summary, release notes, postmortem, attribution record. It is the input to the next Signal or Work item.
proposed_vocabulary.examples_in_tools: Agent run summary / PR description, release notes, postmortem doc, DORA/VSM dashboard, Agent Trace record in git notes
proposed_vocabulary.standard_term: Agent Trace trace record (code to agent conversation attribution); SLSA provenance byproducts (logs); CDEvents links/chainId for end-to-end trace; ITIL problem record / post-incident review

result.notes:
The standards agree on a split between nouns and transitions. CDEvents writes every event as subject + predicate ('change merged', 'service deployed', 'incident detected'). For the user's diagram question, the reading rule follows from that. Boxes are the nouns above, and each is one record kept in some tool. Arrows are predicates: an event that turns one noun into the next or changes its state. Chain from left to right: Signal -> Work item -> (Spec, Plan) -> Agent run -> Change set -> Pipeline run -> Check result + Review -> Verdict -> Build artifact -> Release -> Deployment -> Incident/Report -> new Signal. A diagram that draws 'Issues' or 'GitHub' as a box is drawing a tool, not a noun. Draw the noun and put the tool in a small label.

Gaps no standard fills, so the pipeline must define them itself:
(1) Spec and Verdict have no CDEvents subject.
(2) Release has no CDEvents subject; artifact.published is the closest.
(3) Agent work is split across three young specs: A2A Task for delegation state, OTel invoke_agent for telemetry (development status), and Agent Trace v0.1.0 RFC (Jan 2026) for code attribution. None of them links an agent session to a Work item or Change set. That link is ours to define, the same way GitLab ties MR to issue with 'Closes #N' and CDEvents with links/chainId.

Recommended linkage keys: work item id on every change set and agent run; commit SHA / change id on every pipeline run and check result; artifact digest (purl) on every release and deployment; deployment id on every incident.
