notations.name: Swimlane / cross-functional flowchart
notations.shows_well: Who acts at each step: one lane per role, so every handoff becomes an arrow that crosses a lane boundary. Stages read left to right. A decision diamond in the Human lane shows exactly where a person decides. Most people can read it with no training. Guides say to keep the lanes few and the flow in one direction.
notations.shows_badly: Artifacts. Plain flowcharts have no symbol for 'the thing that moves' (work item, PR), so readers can't see what crosses each arrow or where it is stored. Loops turn into tangled back-arrows unless you label and route them carefully. It also has no time or wait data.
notations.example: Lanes: Human / Agent / Script-CI. 'Triage' (Human) -> 'Implement' (Agent) -> 'Lint+test' (Script) -> 'Review' (Human diamond: approve / request changes -> back-arrow to Implement).

notations.name: BPMN 2.0 (pools, lanes, data objects, data stores, gateways)
notations.shows_well: Covers all six questions with standard symbols. Lanes show actors. Gateways (diamonds) show decisions. Data objects (a page icon with a [state] label) show artifacts going into and out of activities, e.g. 'PR [draft]' -> 'PR [approved]'. Data stores (cylinders) show where artifacts live, such as an issue tracker or repo. Message flows link separate pools, such as an external tracker. Loops are explicit. The bpmn.io community notes that coupling processes through data stores rather than direct messages is a typical pattern, and that fits an agent pipeline that coordinates through a tracker and a repo.
notations.shows_badly: Dense and has many symbols. A reader who doesn't know BPMN will miss the difference between data associations and sequence flow. Diagrams grow quickly. There is no time dimension and no standard way to tell an LLM agent from a script (you have to add your own lane or task-type marker).
notations.example: Pool 'Delivery'. Lanes Human / Agent / CI. Data store 'Work tracker' -> data object 'Issue [ready]' -> Agent task 'Implement' -> data object 'Change set [draft PR]' -> CI service task -> exclusive gateway 'checks pass?' -> Human user task 'Review' -> 'Change set [merged]' -> data store 'Repo main'.

notations.name: Service blueprint
notations.shows_well: Horizontal rows by visibility layer (customer actions, frontstage, a line of visibility, backstage, support processes) under columns that follow the journey left to right. This maps well to 'human-visible layer vs agent backstage vs deterministic infrastructure (support processes)'. It makes plain which steps a human sees and touches and which happen unseen.
notations.shows_badly: Built for customer services, not for change sets. Artifacts and stores are not first-class, and loops and retries are awkward. People read it as a UX artifact, not an engineering contract.
notations.example: Columns: Request / Plan / Build / Verify / Review / Ship. Rows: Owner actions; Visible surfaces (tracker card, PR page); line of visibility; Agent work; Scripts/CI/infra.

notations.name: Value stream map (VSM)
notations.shows_well: Stages in order with process time vs wait time per stage and a lead-time ladder along the bottom. It also shows both the material flow (the artifact) and the information flow (signals, tickets). It is the best tool for finding where work sits waiting, for example a PR queued for human review. Harness and Atlassian have adapted it for software delivery.
notations.shows_badly: It shows actors only weakly, and decisions and branching barely at all. It is a measurement snapshot, not a control-flow spec, and it has no notation for agent vs script.
notations.example: Boxes: Backlog -> Spec -> Implement -> CI -> Review -> Deploy, each with PT/LT. Bottom ladder shows Review wait = 70% of lead time.

notations.name: Kanban board / flow (Kanban Guide 'Definition of Workflow')
notations.shows_well: Where each work item is right now. Columns are explicit states with defined start and finish points, and cards are the work items. WIP limits and queue columns (e.g. 'Ready for review') make waiting and bottlenecks obvious. It is the natural runtime view of a tracker such as Issues/Linear/Jira, and it is not tied to any tool.
notations.shows_badly: No actors (unless card avatars or swimlane rows are added). No artifacts other than the card itself; the PR is just a link on the card. No decision logic. Loops show up only as cards moving backward.
notations.example: Columns: Inbox | Ready (spec approved) | Agent working | Checks | Human review | Done. Card = work item; a PR badge appears on the card from 'Agent working' onward.

notations.name: C4 dynamic diagram
notations.shows_well: Numbered interactions between architecture elements (tracker, orchestrator, agent runner, repo host, CI) for one use case. Good for showing which systems talk to which, in what order.
notations.shows_badly: The C4 docs themselves say to use it sparingly. Its unit is a system or container, not a stage or an artifact. Actors are just boxes, and human decisions and loops do not stand out. It is the wrong level for an overview of the process.
notations.example: 1. Tracker -> Orchestrator: issue labeled 'agent'. 2. Orchestrator -> Agent runner: start run. 3. Agent -> Repo host: push branch / open draft PR. 4. Repo host -> CI: run checks. 5. CI -> Orchestrator: status.

notations.name: CI tool pipeline graph (stages + jobs DAG)
notations.shows_well: The deterministic part, read precisely: stages in columns, jobs as nodes, 'needs' edges as a DAG, live pass/fail status. People already know how to read it.
notations.shows_badly: Shows only scripts. It has no humans (beyond manual-approval jobs), no agents and no upstream work item or spec, and it is scoped to one change set. Feedback to the author is out of view.
notations.example: build -> {unit, lint, typecheck} -> integration -> deploy-staging -> [manual] deploy-prod.

notations.name: Agent workflow / state-machine diagram (Stripe 'blueprint', Anthropic workflow patterns)
notations.shows_well: The inside of an agent run. Shape tells you the kind of actor: Stripe draws deterministic nodes as rectangles and agentic subtasks as clouds. Loops are explicit and bounded (lint loop; at most 2 CI rounds, then hand back to the human). This is the best way to show 'agent vs script' at the step level.
notations.shows_badly: Covers one run only. It doesn't show the work item's life before and after the run, the store where artifacts live, or decisions made by other humans. On its own it is not an overview.
notations.example: [Hydrate context] -> (Implement task) -> [Run linters] <-loop-> (Fix lint) -> [Push] -> [CI] -> (Fix CI failures) x1 -> [Push] -> hand to human.

how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.description: Described as a linear story: Slack message (or ticket/docs/feature-flag UI button) -> isolated devbox -> agent run -> branch -> CI -> PR in the Stripe template -> human review, with no interaction in between. Part 2 (https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents-part-2) shows the 'blueprint' as a state machine diagram whose caption says deterministic nodes are rectangles and agentic subtasks are cloud shapes (e.g. 'Implement task', 'Fix CI failures' as agents; 'Run configured linters', 'Push changes' as code). Loops are bounded and stated: a local lint loop before push, then at most two CI rounds, then the branch goes back to the human operator. The human decides at two points: the trigger, and PR review (approve, request another reviewer, or give the minion more instructions). Stripe says it has more than 1,300 PRs merged per week.

how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.source: AWS — AI-Driven Development Life Cycle (AI-DLC) launch blog (2025) and the open-sourced adaptive workflows blog (figure dated 2025-11)
how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.description: Two levels. Overview: three phases left to right (Inception -> Construction -> Operations), each producing artifacts (requirements, stories, 'Units of Work', designs, code, IaC) that are kept in the project repository as persistent context. Drill-down: Figure 1 is a circular loop that alternates actor icons, with an orange person for Human and a blue brain for AI: Human provides task -> AI creates plan and asks for clarification -> Human clarifies -> AI refines plan -> Human approves plan -> AI executes -> Human verifies outcome. The color/icon per actor makes the human gates explicit. Rituals are named ('Mob Elaboration', 'Mob Construction'), and 'bolts' replace sprints. Launch post: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/ai-driven-development-life-cycle/ ; rules repo: https://github.com/awslabs/aidlc-workflows

Framed as a numbered artifact lifecycle rather than a box diagram: assign an Issue -> the agent opens a draft PR tagged [WIP] and pushes commits as it goes -> it updates the PR title and description and tags you for review -> you comment @copilot to iterate. The PR itself is the work log and the place where feedback happens. Human gates are stated as rules: PRs from the agent need human approval before any CI/CD workflow runs, and branch protections apply. Execution runs in an ephemeral GitHub Actions environment.

how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.source: Cognition — How Cognition Uses Devin to Build Devin (cognition.com blog, 2026)
how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.description: Organized by entry point and trigger rather than one diagram: Slack / Linear-Jira ticket / web / CLI / API events (Sentry crash, failed deploy, a 'Bug' label added) start a session -> Devin plans, codes and opens a PR -> Devin Review organizes the diff and flags bugs by confidence -> Autofix loops on review comments and CI/lint until checks pass -> a human reviews. Ticket-centric automations post results back to the ticket (e.g. a triage summary to Linear), and a daily audit creates tickets plus optional fix PRs. The post says 659 Devin PRs were merged in one week. The figures are product screenshots, not a notation.

how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.source: Anthropic — Effective harnesses for long-running agents (2025-11)
how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.description: Pipeline shown through its artifacts. An initializer agent writes feature_list.json (every feature starts as 'passes: false'), claude-progress.txt, init.sh and an initial git commit. Each later coding-agent session reads progress + git log + feature list, picks one feature, verifies end to end, then commits and updates progress. A table maps each failure mode to initializer behavior vs coding-agent behavior. Lesson for diagrams: draw the handoff artifacts between sessions as first-class objects. Companion: Building effective agents (2024-12, https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents), which draws workflows as In -> LLM call boxes -> gates -> Out, and the evaluator-optimizer as a loop labeled with accepted vs rejected + feedback.

how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.source: Spotify — Background coding agent series (Honk / Fleet Management), Part 1 (2025-11) and Part 3 on feedback loops (2025-12)
how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.description: Fleet-wide pipeline: Fleet Management selects repos -> the background agent makes the change -> a verification loop of deterministic verifiers (format, build, test) plus an LLM-as-judge layer -> PR -> human merge. They draw verifiers as explicit gates before a change is committed. Part 1 says more than 1,500 merged AI-generated PRs: https://engineering.atspotify.com/2025/11/spotifys-background-coding-agent-part-1

Shown only at marketing level: 'From issue to PR automatically'. Droids are pointed at Linear, Jira or GitHub issues and return PRs with code, tests and docs, plus automated review/security scan droids on PRs. I found no primary-source engineering diagram of their pipeline notation (not checked: talks and videos).

how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.source: Martin Fowler site — Understanding Spec-Driven Development: Kiro, spec-kit, Tessl (Birgitta Böckeler, 2025)
how_leaders_draw_agent_pipelines.description: A practitioner comparison of spec-first agent workflows. All three tools use the same artifact chain: requirements -> design -> tasks -> code, with the spec as the main artifact a human reviews. It is useful for deciding where the 'spec' artifact sits in the overview and which human gate approves it.

result.recommendation:
Use one overview: a swimlane with stage columns and an artifact rail. It combines a swimlane, a service blueprint and BPMN data objects, and two drill-down views sit underneath it.

OVERVIEW (one page, read left to right):
1. Columns are stages, 5 to 7 at most, e.g. Intake -> Shape/Spec -> Build -> Verify -> Review -> Release -> Learn. Put each column's name and its 'done when' condition in the header.
2. Lanes are actor types, not tools: Human (owner/reviewer), Agent (LLM), Script/CI (deterministic). Lane = who acts. Back it up with a shape for each actor type (Stripe's convention): rounded/cloud = agent, sharp rectangle = script, person icon or diamond = human. Use one accent color for the Human lane only, as AWS does with orange person icons.
3. An artifact rail runs along the bottom. Draw one row of stores as cylinders, named generically: Work-item store (issues/tickets), Spec store, Change-set store (branch + PR), Build/artifact store, Release/environment. Each step connects to the rail with a dotted line to the artifact it reads or writes. Write the artifact as a document icon with a [state] label (BPMN data-object style), so the reader follows one object changing state: Work item [ready] -> Spec [approved] -> Change set [draft] -> [checks green] -> [approved] -> [merged] -> Release [v1.2]. This answers 'where are the tasks, where is the PR' in a tool-neutral way: GitHub Issues/Linear/Jira are just implementations of the Work-item store, and a PR/MR is an implementation of the Change set.
4. Human decisions are diamonds in the Human lane, with a gate name and its outcomes (e.g. 'Approve spec? yes / revise', 'Merge? approve / request changes / reject'). Keep them few (2 or 3), and make each one a place where a person actually has to decide.
5. Feedback loops are dashed back-arrows in a second color. Label each one with what flows back and its bound: 'CI failure -> Agent, max 2 rounds' (Stripe), 'review comments -> Agent', 'prod incident -> new Work item', 'retro -> rules/playbooks'. Each loop returns to a named stage, never just 'back'.
6. Optionally add a thin row under the columns for wait time vs work time per stage (from VSM) once you have real numbers.

DRILL-DOWN 1, one per agent-heavy stage (Build/Verify): a Stripe-style blueprint, i.e. a state machine with rectangles for script nodes, clouds for agent nodes, and bounded loops with counts, ending in a handoff to the next lane. This is where you show 'agent vs script' in detail without cluttering the overview.

DRILL-DOWN 2, runtime state: a Kanban board whose columns mirror the overview stages, so a card (work item) always sits in exactly one column, with a change-set badge from Build onward. The overview says how it should flow; the board shows where things actually are now.

Use C4 dynamic or system diagrams only as an appendix for 'which systems talk to which', and reuse the CI tool's own pipeline graph for inside the Verify box. Use BPMN as the precise source only if you need executable rigor; for human readers, use the simplified overview above.

Reading rule to give readers in a legend: lane = who; column = when; shape = kind of actor; document with [state] = what moves; cylinder = where it lives; diamond = a human decides; dashed arrow = feedback.

Sources and gaps: searched via fetchira (serper) and read the Stripe, AWS, GitHub, Cognition, Anthropic and C4 pages directly. The Spotify, Factory, BPMN, NN/g, Kanban Guide, VSM and swimlane descriptions come from search snippets and URLs only (not opened). I did not watch the user's YouTube videos.

canonical_stages.name: 1. Intake and triage
canonical_stages.purpose: Turn a raw signal (bug report, alert, request, idea, failed CI, stale flag) into one accepted unit of tracked work, or drop it. Work starts wherever people already talk.
canonical_stages.who: Human usually decides; deterministic triggers (labels, webhooks, cron, alert rules) increasingly start runs automatically.
inputs: Signal (Slack message, ticket, Sentry/Datadog alert, CVE, stale feature flag, CI failure)
outputs: Work item (issue/ticket/bead) or a started Agent run
canonical_stages.human_gate: Human chooses what to delegate (tags the agent, assigns the issue, applies a label). GitHub only accepts triggers from write-access users. Fully automatic triggers exist (Uber AutoClean, Cognition API/label automations, Linear Loops, Microsoft SRE agent opening issues).

canonical_stages.name: 2. Shape: clarify and write the spec
canonical_stages.purpose: Fix intent before any code: the agent asks clarifying questions, then intent, acceptance criteria, constraints and 'what must not change' are written down so a reviewer can later judge the result against them.
canonical_stages.who: Agent interviews and drafts; human answers and decides scope.
outputs: Spec (intent.md/spec.md/requirements.md/acceptance criteria in the issue body)
canonical_stages.human_gate: Human approves the spec (product owner in Anthropic playbook; team 'Mob Elaboration' in AWS AI-DLC; Coinbase treats the plan as a contract). Light-weight sources skip this and use the Slack thread or issue text as the spec.
sources: Anthropic Claude Code best practices (spec by interview)

canonical_stages.name: 3. Plan and decompose
canonical_stages.purpose: Decide how: which files, order, risks, and how completion will be proven (tests). Large work is split into small, isolated units, each small enough for one agent session.
canonical_stages.who: Agent drafts (often in read-only plan mode); human approves; for big work an orchestrator agent splits it.
outputs: Plan (plan.md, task list, units of work, exec plan with verification section)
canonical_stages.human_gate: Plan approval before code (mandatory in Jules and Antigravity; explicit in Anthropic playbook, Factory, AWS AI-DLC; HumanLayer puts its highest-leverage review here on research/design).

canonical_stages.name: 4. Implement in an isolated sandbox
canonical_stages.purpose: An agent writes the change inside a disposable, pre-warmed, full dev environment with only scoped access, so isolation replaces per-action permission prompts.
canonical_stages.human_gate: None during the run in most pipelines; some allow optional live steering (Ramp/Shopify multiplayer, Linear elicitation) or watching the first minute (Anthropic).

canonical_stages.name: 5. Self-verification loop
canonical_stages.purpose: The agent must prove the change works before anyone looks: tests, lint, type checks, build, and often runtime evidence (screenshots, videos, logs). Failures feed straight back to the agent, with bounded retries.
canonical_stages.who: Deterministic tools (test runner, linter, compiler, CI) plus the agent fixing failures.
canonical_stages.human_gate: None; loops are capped (Stripe max 2 CI rounds; Spotify 10 turns/3 retries; Airbnb N retries) and then hand back to a human.

canonical_stages.name: 6. Automated (AI) review and autofix
canonical_stages.purpose: Before any human, one or more reviewer agents check the change against the spec and team standards; a fixer agent addresses findings. Filters remove noise so only real issues reach people.
canonical_stages.who: Reviewer agents (often several specialised ones plus a judge) and the authoring agent fixing.
canonical_stages.human_gate: Normally none; agent approvals do not count as human approvals (Anthropic, GitHub). Escape hatches exist ('break glass' at Cloudflare; request human review at Intercom).

canonical_stages.name: 7. Human review and merge gate
canonical_stages.purpose: A person who did not request the work judges intent, risk and evidence, then the change merges under branch protection / merge queue. Depth of review is increasingly set by risk.
canonical_stages.who: Human code owner plus deterministic merge rules (required checks, branch protection, merge queue).
inputs: Change set with checks green, review findings, evidence
canonical_stages.human_gate: The main gate in most sources. Requester cannot approve own agent PR (GitHub, Ramp via user token). Risk-tiered at Anthropic and Coinbase. Removed for a share of PRs at Intercom (19% AI-approved), OpenAI harness team, Cognition (by default), Gas Town.

canonical_stages.name: 8. Release, deploy and watch
canonical_stages.purpose: Ship behind flags or staged channels, monitor telemetry against a baseline, roll back fast. Agents may watch and propose reverts; production actions stay with a named human.
canonical_stages.who: Deterministic deploy pipeline; monitoring agents; human on-call or the shipper.
canonical_stages.human_gate: Named human for production (Anthropic playbook); human approves revert PR (Cursor Rollouts); approval to restart prod services or merge (AWS AI-DLC); shipper accountable after merge (Intercom, Anthropic 'you land it, you own it').
sources: Intercom (12 min to prod, shipper watches)

canonical_stages.name: 9. Learn and close the loop
canonical_stages.purpose: Incidents, misses, review comments and agent traces become new work items, new checks/lint rules, updated agent instructions and eval cases for the agents themselves.
canonical_stages.who: Scheduled agents propose; humans decide what to adopt.
canonical_stages.human_gate: Humans pick which proposals to adopt and triage new work items.
sources: Anthropic playbook (metrics -> new intent.md; evals in CI)
OpenAI (garbage collection, promote rule into code)
Cursor Cloud Doctor, Bugbot learned rules

artifacts.name: Signal
artifacts.definition: Raw input that might become work, not yet accepted: alert, error spike, user feedback, CVE, chat request, idea.
artifacts.tool_examples: Slack message, Sentry/Datadog alert, PagerDuty event, Zendesk ticket, Dependabot advisory, stale feature flag record

artifacts.name: Work item
artifacts.definition: Accepted, tracked unit of work with one owner, a state and a type (feature/defect/risk/debt). Everything downstream links back to its id.
artifacts.tool_examples: GitHub Issue, Jira work item, Linear issue, GitLab issue, Beads bead, Codex task queue entry

artifacts.name: Spec
artifacts.definition: What 'done' means: intent, acceptance criteria, constraints, what must not change. Reviewers and verifiers judge against it.
artifacts.tool_examples: intent.md/spec.md/requirements.md, issue body with acceptance criteria, PRD/RFC/ADR, Spotify migration prompt

artifacts.name: Plan
artifacts.definition: How the work will be done: ordered steps, files, risks and required proof, written before code; may split into sub-items.
artifacts.tool_examples: plan.md, exec-plans/, sub-issues, AI-DLC units of work, Factory mission milestones, agent plan checklist

artifacts.name: Agent configuration (project memory)
artifacts.definition: Standing instructions, procedures, tools and hard guardrails every agent run loads; separate from the per-change spec.
artifacts.tool_examples: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, Cursor rules, skills/playbooks, MCP tool registry (Stripe Toolshed), hooks, deny rules

artifacts.name: Agent run (session)
artifacts.definition: One execution by an agent on a work item, in a sandbox, with transcript, tool calls, cost and final state (completed/failed/needs input).
artifacts.tool_examples: Claude Code/Codex/Copilot/Devin session, Linear AgentSession, A2A Task, Shopify session event log

artifacts.name: Sandbox
artifacts.definition: Isolated, disposable environment with the full toolchain where the agent runs and tests; limits blast radius.
artifacts.tool_examples: Stripe devbox, Modal snapshot, Firecracker microVM, git worktree, GitHub Actions runner, Cursor cloud VM

artifacts.name: Change set
artifacts.definition: Proposed, reviewable modification on a branch targeting a base, linked to its work item; merged or abandoned.
artifacts.tool_examples: GitHub pull request, GitLab merge request, Gerrit change, Google CL, Phabricator diff

artifacts.name: Check result
artifacts.definition: Machine outcome of one automated check against a change set: pass/fail plus details.
artifacts.tool_examples: CI job status, test report, lint/typecheck output, CodeQL/secret scan, GitHub check run

artifacts.name: Verification evidence
artifacts.definition: Proof the change behaves as intended, attached for humans: commands with output, screenshots, recordings, API responses.
artifacts.tool_examples: PR screenshots, Devin/Cursor demo videos, Showboat document, Abnormal testbox evidence

artifacts.name: Review
artifacts.definition: Judgement on a change set by a person or agent (approve/request changes/comment) with line-level findings; differs from a check because someone judged it.
artifacts.tool_examples: GitHub PR review, Anthropic Code Review findings, Bugbot, uReview, CodeRabbit, Gerrit vote

artifacts.name: Verdict (gate decision)
artifacts.definition: The single go/no-go for a transition (merge, release, promote), naming who decided on what evidence.
artifacts.tool_examples: Branch protection + required checks, merge queue result, Anthropic risk-tier approval, Cloudflare approve/block, deploy protection rule

artifacts.name: Release / Deployment
artifacts.definition: Release: a versioned set of artifacts declared ready. Deployment: a specific version put into a specific environment, with outcome (succeeded/rolled back).
artifacts.tool_examples: git tag + GitHub Release, feature flag rollout, latest/stable channel, Argo CD sync, Dokploy deploy

artifacts.name: Incident
artifacts.definition: Confirmed unplanned degradation of a running service, linked to the deployment that likely caused it and the follow-up work items.
artifacts.tool_examples: PagerDuty/Opsgenie incident, Meta SEV, Jira Service Management incident, Sentry escalated issue

artifacts.name: Eval suite
artifacts.definition: Regression tests for the agents themselves, built from real past tasks and incidents; rerun when model, prompt or rule changes.
artifacts.tool_examples: Anthropic playbook 20-50 past tasks, Anthropic incident PRs scoring the reviewer, DoorDash incident eval set, Uber benchmarks

consensus.statement: Writing code is no longer the bottleneck; review, verification, CI capacity and human attention are. Pipelines are redesigned around that.
Every change ends as a reviewable change set (PR/MR/CL/diff); the existing review and merge path is kept and agents are plugged into it.
Agents run in isolated, pre-warmed, full dev environments; isolation replaces per-action permission prompts.
Closed, fast, deterministic feedback (tests, lint, build, CI) is the main quality driver; the agent must not report done until checks are green, and retry loops are bounded.
Deterministic code handles anything predictable (targeting, git, push, lint, validation); the LLM handles only the fuzzy middle.
sources: Anthropic best practices (soft vs hard controls)

consensus.statement: An automated AI review runs on every change before a human, and it is filtered for precision (severity tags, judges, dedup, suppressing style nits).
The reviewer must be independent of the author: fresh-context reviewer agent, agent approvals do not count as human approvals, the requester cannot approve their own agent's PR.
sources: Anthropic playbook (author agent never approves itself)

consensus.statement: Write intent down before code (spec and/or plan), keep tasks small and well-scoped; success scales with specificity.
Persistent knowledge lives in the repo or config as short instruction files and reusable procedures, loaded on demand, and kept up to date from failures.
Reviewing runtime evidence (screenshots, videos, test output) is replacing or supplementing line-by-line code reading.
The loop closes: incidents, misses and traces become new work items, new checks/rules and eval cases for the agents.
Small batches and fast revert are the safety net; AI amplifies existing practice, so without automated tests and version control more volume means less stability.

divergences.question: Must a human approve every merge?
divergences.side_a: Yes, a human (not the requester) approves: Stripe, Ramp, Brex, Spotify, Google, Uber, GitHub, Linear, Monzo, Cloudflare ('AI review is not a replacement'), DoorDash (AI advisory), AWS AI-DLC, Anthropic best practices.
divergences.side_b: Not always: Intercom lets AI approve ~19% of PRs; OpenAI harness team lets agents merge their own PRs; Cognition merges bug-to-merge with no human by default; Anthropic monorepo moves to auto-merge for low-risk with risk tiers; Gas Town (Refinery agent) and Ralph push directly.

divergences.question: How heavy should the spec/planning stage be?
divergences.side_a: Heavy, staged artifacts with approvals: AWS AI-DLC (33 stages), spec-kit/Kiro, Anthropic playbook (intent -> spec -> plan), Coinbase (plan as contract, fix spec not code), Factory (most value in planning), HumanLayer QRSPI (8 steps).
divergences.side_b: Light: Stripe/Cognition/Shopify start from a Slack message; OpenAI Codex team writes very few specs; Böckeler finds spec-kit slower than plain coding on small stories and 'would rather review code than markdown'; AWS and HumanLayer themselves moved to adaptive depth.

divergences.question: Where should the main human gate sit?
divergences.side_a: Upstream, on research/design/plan before code: HumanLayer, Factory, AWS AI-DLC, Coinbase, Jules, Antigravity, Abnormal (design settled in plan).
divergences.side_b: Downstream, at the PR: GitHub, Linear, Stripe, Brex, Spotify, Google; or after merge (Intercom shipper watches prod; Anthropic monorepo post-merge testing).

divergences.question: What does the human review: code or evidence?
divergences.side_a: Read and own the code: Osmani ('never commit code you can't explain'), Willison, HumanLayer 2026, Böckeler.
divergences.side_b: Review evidence or harness output: Cognition (videos instead of IDE), Cursor (demo artifacts), Abnormal (runtime evidence), Datadog (DST/TLA+ harness replaces code review as correctness source).

divergences.question: How much context and how many tools should an agent get?
divergences.side_a: Narrow: Spotify (no code search, few tools, static prompts), Stripe (curated subset of ~500 tools), DoorDash ('focused context beats more context').
divergences.side_b: Rich: Uber Context Graph (24M nodes) with 1,000+ MCP tools behind a gateway; Ramp ('limited only by model intelligence, not missing context').

divergences.question: How to structure the AI reviewer?
divergences.side_a: Fan-out of single-property/specialist reviewers plus coordinator: Cloudflare (up to 7), Intercom sub-agents, Uber CodeCourt (found one end-to-end reviewer worse), Amp (one agent per check).
divergences.side_b: DoorDash found specialist fan-out misses architectural issues and moved to scout + 2 deep reviewers + falsification; Spotify uses a single judge.

divergences.question: Parallel swarms or one agent at a time?
divergences.side_a: Parallel: Cognition managed Devins, Yegge Gas Town (20-30 agents), OpenAI engineers 4-8 parallel agents, Cursor research harness (hundreds).
divergences.side_b: Serial/monolith: Factory found serial with targeted parallelism better; Huntley Ralph monolith; HumanLayer uses sub-agents only for context control.

divergences.question: Where is the hub of the pipeline (where work items live)?
divergences.side_a: The tracker: Linear (AgentSession protocol), GitHub (issue = prompt), Gas Town (Beads in git), Abnormal (ticket tags).
divergences.side_b: Chat/session: Stripe, Shopify, Cognition, Amp threads; or repo files: AWS aidlc-docs, OpenAI exec-plans, Ralph fix_plan.md. Several big-company sources describe no tracker stage at all.

divergences.question: Pre-merge or post-merge testing at high volume?
divergences.side_a: Pre-merge gates: Stripe pre-push lint + CI, Claude Code repos merge queue, GitHub human-approved CI.
divergences.side_b: Anthropic monorepo dropped the global merge-queue lock at 30K merges/day for post-merge/pre-deploy testing; OpenAI harness keeps minimal blocking gates ('corrections are cheap, waiting is expensive').

synth.human_touchpoints:
Where humans stay across almost all sources: (1) deciding what to build and starting the run (tagging/assigning/labelling; Anthropic: 'starting the run, defining done, approving the merge' are the three things the human keeps); (2) defining done: approving the spec or plan, owning acceptance criteria and architecture trade-offs (AWS, Anthropic playbook, Coinbase, Factory, HumanLayer, Jules, OpenAI harness 'humans steer, agents execute'); (3) the merge verdict, made by someone other than the requester (GitHub, Ramp, Brex, Stripe, Spotify, Google, Uber, Cloudflare, Monzo, Linear); (4) production and irreversible actions: named approver for prod, approving reverts, restarting services, money-moving changes (Anthropic playbook, AWS AI-DLC, Cursor Rollouts, Coinbase); (5) deciding which agent-proposed improvements to adopt and what to codify into rules (Cognition, OpenAI, Cursor, Willison).

Where humans were removed and why: (a) as messengers in the feedback loop: Brex replaced humans relaying CI and review-bot output with three scripts; Stripe and Spotify run fully unattended until the PR; (b) as first-pass reviewers: AI review runs before any human everywhere, and Uber abandons failing diffs before a human sees them, because human review capacity is the bottleneck (Google throttled output to reviewer speed); (c) as line-by-line readers: replaced by evidence (Cognition, Cursor, Abnormal) or verification harnesses (Datadog), justified by volume; (d) as approvers for low-risk changes: Intercom auto-approves ~19% of PRs citing measured revert rates and SOC2/HIPAA audit logging, Anthropic moves toward auto-merge of low-risk changes by risk classifier, OpenAI harness team makes human review optional; (e) Meta moved to 'human-on-the-loop': engineers set criteria and review aggregates, and authors only answer 'was this intended?' for top-ranked catches. In every case an escape hatch remains (break glass, request human review, escalation), and accountability is moved to the shipper or operator rather than abolished.

synth.diagram_recommendation:
The user's confusion ('where are the tasks, where is the PR') comes from diagrams that mix tools, stages and actors in one kind of box. Use one rule: boxes are nouns (artifacts), arrows are transitions (events), lanes are who. The tool name (GitHub Issues, Linear, Jira) is only a small grey label on the store, never the box itself.

Overview = swimlane with stage columns plus an artifact rail (a simplified mix of swimlane, service blueprint and BPMN data objects):
1. Columns left to right = stages, 6-8 at most: Intake -> Shape (spec) -> Plan -> Build -> Verify -> Review & merge -> Release & watch -> Learn. Each header gets a one-line 'done when'.
2. Three lanes = actor type, not tool: Human, Agent (LLM), Script/CI (deterministic). Reinforce with shape (Stripe convention): cloud/rounded = agent, sharp rectangle = script, person icon = human. Only the Human lane gets an accent colour (AWS uses orange person icons) so gates jump out.
3. Artifact rail along the bottom: cylinders for stores, named generically (Work-item store, Spec/plan files, Change-set store, CI results, Release/environment), each with the tool as a small label. Above the rail, follow ONE object changing state with document icons: Work item [ready] -> Spec [approved] -> Plan [approved] -> Change set [draft] -> [checks green] -> [AI-reviewed] -> [approved] -> [merged] -> Release [vX] -> Deployment [live]. Steps connect to what they read/write with dotted lines. This directly answers 'where are tasks' (Work-item store) and 'where is the PR' (Change-set store).
4. Human decisions = diamonds in the Human lane with a gate name and outcomes ('Approve spec? yes/revise', 'Merge? approve/request changes/reject', 'Prod deploy? go/rollback'). Keep 2-4, only where a person really decides.
5. Feedback loops = dashed back-arrows in a second colour, each labelled with what flows back and its bound: 'check failure -> Agent, max 2 rounds', 'review findings -> Agent', 'incident -> new Work item', 'miss -> new rule/eval'. Each returns to a named stage.
6. A legend on the page: lane = who; column = when; shape = kind of actor; document [state] = what moves; cylinder = where it lives; diamond = a human decides; dashed arrow = feedback.

Drill-downs, not on the overview: (a) Stripe-style blueprint state machine for Build/Verify (rectangles = script nodes, clouds = agent nodes, bounded loops with counts); (b) a Kanban board whose columns mirror the overview stages, showing where each work item is right now, with a change-set badge from Build onward; (c) optional C4 dynamic diagram as an appendix for which systems talk to which. Avoid full BPMN for human readers; it is precise but too dense.
open_doubts: Almost every number is a vendor or company self-report with no published method; only METR (RCT) and DORA (survey) are independent measurements, and both are more cautious than the vendors.

Metrics are not comparable: 'no human-written code' (Stripe), 'merged PRs written by' (Ramp, whose definition shifted over time), 'coauthored' (Shopify 1 in 8), 'PRs created by agents' (Coinbase via Cursor), 'merged PRs' (Cognition 40x, Cursor 56% with undisclosed counting).
No organisation published a run success rate (share of agent runs that never become a merged PR), so throughput claims hide the abandon rate.
Intercom's revert-rate comparison (0.53% vs 5.39%) is not controlled for task difficulty; agents may get easier changes.
Cognition's 40x merged PRs / 10x productivity and 'just as high quality' are a vendor talk with no method; review and merge gates are not described.
Coinbase figures (20-25 days to 1.8 days, 75% of PRs by agents) come from vendor write-ups (Arize, Cursor), not a Coinbase engineering post.

AWS AI-DLC speed claims (5-20x in the video, 10-15x at re:Invent) are unsourced; a secondary source says the Operations phase is still a placeholder in the open-source spec, though the video presents it as complete.
Anthropic's 30,000 merges/day figure was reported via secondary coverage of a chart; the code review post was read via an X republication, not the original page.
The third-party video 6CaQ9ZFuuKI plays down the human gates that Anthropic's own course specifies, and implies AI can review and merge; the IBM video slightly misquotes METR (20% vs 19%).

OpenAI's 'agents merge their own PRs, human review optional' is one greenfield team with unlimited tokens; the authors say it may not generalise, and no defect or revert data is given. Codex-team details come from a secondary interview.
Gas Town and Ralph are explicitly not recommended by their own authors (Yegge: 'do not use Gas Town'; Huntley: never on an existing codebase).
Böckeler's critique (heavy spec ceremony slower than coding on small tasks, agents ignore specs) contradicts the spec-heavy vendors and has not been answered with data.

DORA's finding that AI hurts stability is in tension with vendor advice to run many parallel agent PRs; no vendor reports stability/change-fail data except Intercom and Anthropic (revert share fell >40%).
The issue-tracker / work-item stage is barely documented by the large companies (most start from Slack); researchers found no source describing it in detail outside Linear, GitHub and Abnormal.
Several dates were not verified on the source pages (YouTube video dates, Kent Beck, Huntley, Airbnb, DoorDash, Abnormal, Datadog posts).
